Surah al-Fath (The Victory)

It was revealed in Medina, according to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both. However, the reports indicate that it was revealed during a journey and not in Medina itself, and this is the sound view. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and a group of others related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "We were returning from al-Hudaybiyah with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in the sixth year after the Hijrah. He had set out for it on Monday, at the beginning of Dhu al-Qa'dah, and he stayed there for some ten-odd days, and it was said twenty days. Then he (peace be upon him) turned back. While we were travelling, the Revelation came to him, and when it came to him it weighed heavily upon him, then it was lifted from him, and in him was such joy as Allah the Exalted willed. He informed us that it had been sent down to him: ﴿Indeed We have granted you a clear victory﴾."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a journey, and I asked him about something three times, but he did not answer me. So I urged my camel forward and went ahead of the people, fearing that something might be revealed concerning me in the Qur'an. I had hardly settled when I heard a crier calling me, so I hurried, thinking that something had been revealed concerning me. Then the Prophet ﷺ said: 'There has been sent down to me tonight a surah more beloved to me than the world and all that is in it: ﴿Indeed We have granted you a clear victory﴾ ﴿That Allah may forgive you your sins, past and future﴾.'"

In a sound hadith related by Ahmad, Abu Dawud and others from Majma' ibn Jariyah al-Ansari, there is what indicates that it was revealed also after his ﷺ departure from al-Hudaybiyah, and that this was at Kura' al-Ghamim, where he (peace be upon him) recited it to the people while he was on his mount. In the narration of Ibn Sa'd from him there is what indicates that it was at Dajnan. This was related from al-Biqa'i. Dajnan, with a dad, jim and two nuns with an alif between them, on the pattern of sakran, as in the Qamus, is a mountain near Makkah. This and similar reports are a view that it was revealed between Makkah and Medina, and such a case is counted as Madani according to the well-known view, namely that the Madani is what was revealed after the Hijrah, whether it was revealed in Medina, in Makkah, or on one of the journeys. The Makki is what was revealed before the Hijrah. As for the view that the Makki is what was revealed even after the Hijrah in Makkah, and that it includes its surroundings, such as Mina, 'Arafat and al-Hudaybiyah, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti said, and indeed some of it according to what is in al-Hidayah, and most of it according to what al-Muhibb al-Tabari said, from the sanctuary (haram) of Makkah; and the Madani is what was revealed in Medina, and it includes its surroundings, such as Uhud, Badr and Sal', as he also said. Then, on the view that it was revealed near Makkah, it is counted as Makki. So the claim that the surah is Madani without any dispute about it is clearly open to question. It has twenty-nine verses by consensus. The fitness of its placement here is not hidden, because victory in the sense of help is connected to fighting; and in each of the mention of the sincere believers, the hypocrites and the polytheists there is something relevant; and the command to seek forgiveness was mentioned in the earlier part, while the occurrence of forgiveness is mentioned here; and the "word of goodness" was mentioned there by its noble wording, and was alluded to by the "word of piety" according to the most famous views concerning it. You will learn of it, Allah willing, and of other matters. In al-Bahr, the aspect of its connection with what precedes it is that when ﴿And if you turn away﴾ and the rest of the verse had preceded, which is an address to the Quraysh disbelievers, Allah the Glorified informed His Messenger ﷺ of the great victory, and that by this victory the exchange took place, and everyone who was in Makkah became secure, and it became a land of faith. There is in this what is not hidden. In the earlier reports there is what indicates the greatness of its rank.

In the hadith of Majma' ibn Jariyah which Ibn Sa'd related from him: "When Jibril, peace be upon him, descended with it there, he said: 'We congratulate you, O Messenger of Allah.' When Jibril, peace be upon him, congratulated him, the Muslims congratulated him." It is also related that whoever recites it on the first night of Ramadan will be protected throughout that year, but this is not established in any sound report, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Indeed We have granted you﴾: it is an informing about the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah according to the majority, and this was related from Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, al-Sha'bi and al-Zuhri. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "And this is the sound view." The root of fath (opening) is the removal of closure. The opening of a land, as in the Kashshaf, is attaining mastery over it either by force or by agreement, or by war or otherwise, because it is closed so long as one has not attained mastery over it; and when one has attained mastery over it and it is in one's hand, it has been opened. That treaty was named a "victory" because the two share in manifestation and dominance over the polytheists, for, as al-Kalbi said, they did not seek a truce until the Muslims had prevailed over them. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the Muslims shot at them, that is with arrows and stones, as it was said, until they drove them into their homes; or because that treaty became a cause for the conquest of Makkah. al-Zuhri said: "There was no victory greater than the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah. The polytheists mixed with the Muslims, heard their speech, and Islam took firm root in their hearts, and in three years a great multitude embraced Islam, and the number of Muslims grew greatly through them." al-Qurtubi said: "Those years had not passed before the Muslims came to Makkah with ten thousand men, and they conquered it." The naming, on the first view, is of the type of metaphor by continuation (isti'arah tab'iyyah) however it is arranged; on the second view it is of the type of metonymy by sending (majaz mursal), whether or not we say that in such a case it is by continuation, since the cause is named by the name of its effect. There is no obstacle to two kinds of relation existing between two things, so that the use of one of them for the other is by consideration of each kind of metaphor, as in al-mishfar and al-shafah al-ghalidhah (the thick lip) for a human being. The attribution of the opening, meaning the treaty which is the act of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, is a metaphor by attributing to the one who receives the act what belongs to the one who brings it into being. There is in that what there is of exalting the matter of the treaty and of the Messenger, peace be upon him. It is not said: it has been established in discourse that all acts are created by Him, the Exalted, so attributing the treaty to Him, the Glorified, is an attribution to what belongs to Him, and so there is no metaphor. For we say: "what belongs to Him" means that the act is what should be attributed to that agent in common usage, whether it is created by Him, the Exalted, or by other than Him, the Mighty and Majestic, as al-Sa'd clearly stated in al-Mutawwal. And how could it not be so, for if it were otherwise, the attribution of all acts to other than Him, the Exalted, would be a metaphor and to Him, the Exalted, would be literal, as with prayer, fasting and others.

al-Muhaqqiq Mirzajan said: "It is possible to construe what is in the noble verse as a concealed metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), or to intend the creation and bringing into being of the treaty, or that the metaphor lies in the compositional form which is laid down for attribution to what belongs to the agent, so that it is used for attribution to other than him, or that it is of the kind of allegorical metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah). The four aspects apply to everything that is of the kind of rational metaphor, like 'the spring made the herbs grow.' The people have clearly stated the first three of them. Some claimed that the treaty is among what is attributed to Him, the Exalted, literally, so it does not need any of that; and there is in this what there is. It is also possible that this is an informing about making the polytheists at al-Hudaybiyah overcome, fearful, and seeking the treaty, with the opening being a metaphor for that, and its attribution to Him, the Exalted, being literal. The fact that what occurred at al-Hudaybiyah was an opening was hidden from some of the Companions until the Prophet, peace be upon him, made it clear."

al-Bayhaqi related from 'Urwah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned from al-Hudaybiyah, and a man from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'By Allah, this is not a victory. We were turned back from the House, our offering was held back, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stopped at al-Hudaybiyah, and two men among the Muslims who had gone out were sent back.' The news reached the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he said: 'Evil is this speech. Rather, this is the greatest of victories. The polytheists have been content that you should repel them with a sword's reach from their lands, and they ask you for a settlement, and they desire from you safety, though they have disliked what they disliked from you. Allah has given you mastery over them, and returned you safe, spoiling and rewarded. This is the greatest of victories. Have you forgotten the Day of Uhud, when you went up and did not turn to anyone while I was calling you from your rear? Have you forgotten the Day of the Confederates, when they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes turned aside and the hearts reached the throats, and you thought about Allah thoughts?' The Muslims said: 'Allah and His Messenger have spoken truly. It is indeed the greatest of victories. By Allah, O Prophet of Allah, we did not think about what you have mentioned, and you are more knowing of Allah and of affairs than we are.'"

The benefit of the informing about the victory, on both aspects, is with respect to others than him, peace be upon him, because he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, knows that, and likewise knows the necessary benefit. So it is said.

Restricting "others" to those who were not present at the opening among the Companions and others is because those present already knew that before the revelation. It was also said: the one present only knew the occurrence of the treaty or that the polytheists were in a state of seeking it, and did not know that it was a victory, as the report suggests. Even if it be granted that he knew that, he did not know the greatness of its matter, as the attribution to the plural of majesty and the informing of it in that respect suggest.

Some verifiers said: perhaps the intended purpose of the information is that this is for forgiveness and what is conjoined to it, so the benefit may also be with respect to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. I say: They have clearly stated that a declarative sentence is often used for purposes other than conveying the judgment or its necessary consequence, like ﴿My Lord, I have given birth to a female﴾, ﴿My Lord, my bones have weakened﴾, ﴿Those who sit back among the believers are not equal﴾ and so on, of what cannot be counted. So the purpose of mentioning it here may be to bestow favour rather than conveying the judgment or its consequence, and there is no metaphor in that or the like, as al-'Allamah 'Abd al-Hakim al-Sialkuti indicated in his glosses on al-Mutawwal.

In al-Risalah al-Jundiyyah it is clearly stated that the declarative compositional form in such cases is transferred to the performative, and that the metaphor lies in the form alone, not in the parts nor in the whole; and it is a single metaphor according to the author of the Risalah, and the word is greater than the literal and the figurative (hukmi) term. Some say it is a compound metaphor and is not restricted to the allegorical kind; its verification is in its proper place.

The emphasis with "inna" is for attention, not to refute denial; it was also said that because the judgment, given the greatness of its matter, is a likely object of denial. It was also said: because some of the hearers deny that what occurred was a victory. And the repetition of the judgment is spoken of in such terms.

Mujahid said: the intended victory is the conquest of Khaybar, which is a large town with fortresses and farms, eight stages from Medina toward the direction of Syria. The departure of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as Ibn Ishaq said and al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar preferred, was in the latter part of Muharram in the seventh year, and he besieged it for some ten-odd nights until he conquered it.

Ibn Hazm also related from Malik, and affirmed, that it occurred at the end of the sixth year. He reconciled this with the view of those who state the sixth year by holding that the beginning of the year is counted from the true month of the Hijrah, which is Rabi' al-Awwal. The statement of Shaykh Abu Hamid in al-Ta'liqah, that the expedition of Khaybar took place in the fifth year, is a mistake. Likewise, the statement of Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abi Shaybah, reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that it took place on the eighteenth of Ramadan, is an error. Perhaps the original reading was "Hunayn," which was then altered, but even so it requires explanation. The conquest was achieved by the hands of the People of al-Hudaybiyah, and none of those who stayed behind from it shared in it. So the "conquest" is in its literal sense, and its attribution to Him, Exalted is as you have heard in what preceded. The emphasis by "inna" and the repetition of the judgment are for the sake of importance. The expression of it in the past tense, although it had not yet occurred on the day of revelation, is based on what is reported from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, that the surah was revealed in its entirety between Makkah and Madinah. This is the metaphorical usage of "approaching" (majaz al-mushārafah), like "he killed a slain man," according to the well-known view, or it is the first kind, like His words: ﴿Indeed I see myself pressing wine﴾ (Yusuf 12:36). Their difference in being a verbal or nominal sentence does no harm. There is another aspect to this, which will become known from what follows, if Allah the Exalted wills.

A group held that it was the conquest of Makkah. According to Zad al-Ma'ad, it was the Greatest Conquest, by which Allah the Exalted exalted His religion, rescued His land, purified His sanctuary, the people of the heavens rejoiced at it, the tent-ropes of its glory were struck upon the shoulders of Orion, after it people entered the religion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in multitudes, and the face of time was illuminated with radiance and joy. It occurred in the eighth year, and in one narration, in the eighth year and a half. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out, according to what Ahmad related with a sound chain from Abu Sa'id, two nights remaining of Ramadan. The conquest of Makkah was on the thirteenth of it, according to what is related from al-Zuhri. It is related from a group that the conquest was in the last ten days of Ramadan. It has been said otherwise as well. With the Messenger of Allah ﷺ there were ten thousand Muslims, and it has been said twelve thousand. The combining of these is possible.

According to al-Shafi'i, the conquest was by treaty (sulh). This is also a narration from Ahmad, granting safety at the pass of Zahran to whoever entered the house of Abu Sufyan, whoever entered the mosque is safe, and because the houses were not divided among the spoils-takers. Most scholars held that it was by force (‘anwah), because of the explicit command to fight, its occurrence at the hand of Khalid ibn al-Walid, and his peace and blessings upon him saying: "A portion of the day was made lawful for me."

Granting safety is not called a treaty (sulh) unless the one addressed by it commits to ceasing fighting. The sound reports make clear that the Quraysh did not commit to this. Leaving the distribution is not necessarily a sign that the conquest was by force, for a town may be taken by force and its people be granted favour, and their houses be left to them.

After the conquest, he, peace be upon him, remained fifteen nights according to the narration of al-Bukhari, seventeen nights according to the narration of Abu Dawud, eighteen nights according to the narration of al-Tirmidhi, and nineteen nights according to the narration of some others. The full discussion is in the books of biography (siyar). Abu Hayyan favoured this view, and mentioned that it suits the end of the preceding surah, when He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Here you are, those who are being called﴾ (Muhammad 47:38). So He, Exalted, made clear that He opened Makkah for them, they gained spoils, and they obtained many times what they had spent, and if they had been stingy, that loss would have fallen upon them, so their stinginess is only against themselves. Also, when He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿You are the superior ones, and Allah is with you﴾ (Muhammad 47:35), He made clear His proof by the conquest of Makkah, for they were then the superior ones. Also, when He, Exalted, said: ﴿So do not weaken and call for peace﴾ (Muhammad 47:35), that was manifest in the conquest of Makkah, since no weakness reached them and they did not call for reconciliation. Rather, the chieftains of Quraysh came seeking safety and submitting. This is clear according to the view that by it is meant the conquest of al-Hudaybiyah. As for the view that by it is meant the conquest of Khaybar, it is not so.

Some scholars preferred the view that it is the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah over the view that it is the conquest of Makkah, on the ground that the promise of the conquest of Makkah comes explicitly in this noble surah, namely His words: ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled the vision of His Messenger with truth. You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ (al-Fath 48:27). So if this conquest is taken to refer to that, it would be an emphasis (ta'kid). But if it is taken to refer to the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, it would be a new information (ta'sis), and new information is better than emphasis. Some preferred it over the view that it is the conquest of Khaybar for the same reason, since the conquest of Khaybar is also mentioned later. There is room for discussion in that matter. As for the repetition, it is for what preceded, and likewise the attribution to the pronoun of greatness. Rather, this conquest is more deserving of attention and of magnifying its importance. So much so that it has been said that its attribution to Him, Exalted, is because it is one of the strange and wondrous matters which Allah creates by the hands of His prophets, peace be upon them, like the throwing of pebbles, referred to by His words: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ (al-Anfal 8:17). This is a manifest error. The well-known view is that there is an intellectual metaphor (majaz 'aqli) in the statement, and in it are the possibilities mentioned earlier.

Some of the verifiers said: It is possible to say that perhaps the intention (irādah) here is considered, either by way of ellipsis (hadhf), or by way of metonymy (majaz mursal), as in His words: ﴿When you stand up for prayer﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:6), and His words: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ (al-Nahl 16:98), according to most of the imams. Like this interpretation, it has been said that it is applicable to voluntary actions. Some claimed that the conquest is a metaphor for facilitating it.

Among the great scholars, in explaining the emphasis, it was mentioned that the non-questioner may be treated as a questioner when something is presented to him that hints at the news. They stated that what is hinted at need not be a speech. Many exegetes and others mentioned that he, peace be upon him, saw in a dream that he and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, entered Makkah in safety. So the situation became one in which the conquest was to be hesitated over, and he, peace and blessings upon him, was addressed with the speech emphasized, as it is addressed to a questioner like that. It was also permitted that it be to refute denial, based on the fact that the polytheists were certain of it, for they used to claim that he, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, would not take control of Makkah, just as no one who had wanted to take control of it before him, peace and blessings be upon him, had done so. But this, as you see, is weak.

Some eminent scholars who held that by it is meant the conquest of Makkah mentioned that the statement is a promise of its conquest. Then it was said that the sentence in that case is an assertion (ikhbar), and it was said that it is a performative (inshā'). This was challenged by what al-Radi stated, that according to inductive investigation, performative sentences are restricted to the imperative and the performative-declarative types, and a promise is neither of these. As for the first, it is obvious. As for the second, a mere statement like "I will certainly honour you" does not by itself accomplish the honouring. Some of the great scholars said: Their discourse is inconsistent on whether the promise is a performative or an assertion, and it is possible to reconcile this by saying that the origin of the promise is a performative, for it is the manifestation of a matter in the soul that makes the addressee happy. What is connected with the promise, which is the promised matter, is an assertion. A similar statement is the grammarians' remark that the particle "ka'anna" (as if) is for performative tashbih, although what follows it is a declarative sentence.

Al-Khafaji said: This arises from a failure to understand what is meant by it. If it is said: What is meant by "I will certainly honour you," for example, is honouring in the future, then it is undoubtedly an assertion. If it is said: Its meaning is the resolve to honour him and the hastening of his joy by informing him, then it is a performative. I say: It is not hidden that assertion is the basis of performative speech, and the scholar al-Taftazani has clearly stated this in al-Mutawwal. The form of the compound does not indicate that it is a performative, and there is nothing in its substance that indicates that. So it may be said that it is an assertion intended to hasten the joy, and that this does not take it out of being an assertion, similar to what was said about His words: ﴿My Lord, I have given birth to a female﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:36) and the like. So reflect.

The expression of it in the past tense is for its certainty. In it is consolation for the hearts of the Companions and the solace of them, since they had become exceedingly grieved over the delay of the conquest, and what it contains.

This expression is among the kinds of metaphor by transference (isti'arah tab'iyyah), as the Sayyid al-Sanad verified in the margins of al-Mutawwal, where he said: Know that the expression of the present tense by the past, and the reverse, is counted as a metaphor, by likening what has not occurred to what has occurred in the certainty of the event, and by likening the past to the present in being before the eyes and necessary to witness. Then the word of one of them is borrowed for the other. Accordingly, the metaphor in the verb is of two kinds. One is that a severe striking is likened to killing, for example, and its name is borrowed for it, and then from it is derived "qutila" in the sense of "was struck a severe blow." The second is that a future striking is likened to a past striking, for example, in the certainty of its occurrence, so "ḍuriba" is used for it. The verbal meaning, namely the striking, is then present in each of the likened and the likened-to, but it is restricted in each of them by a qualifier that differs from the other, so the comparison is valid for that reason.

The verifier Mirzajan said: It is possible to explain the metaphor here in another way, namely that the future time is likened to the past time, the aspect of resemblance being that just as the second is the container of a matter certain to occur, so too is the first time. The word indicating the second time, namely the past verb, has been made, by its form, to indicate the future time and to be used for it. It is clear that the verbal noun (maṣdar) remains as it was, its meaning unchanged. So the metaphor in the form and the pattern is more fitting, because it is that which indicates the past time, and through it the metaphor is in the verb, just as the metaphor is in the verb by means of the verbal noun. The difference is that this metaphor in the verb is through its essence and root, whereas in our case it is through its form. It cannot be said that what indicates time is the word itself derived, not part of it, for we say: this possibility also applies to the well-known metaphor by transference, by saying that what indicates the event-meaning is the derived word itself and not part of it, because the verbal noun in its form is not realized in the derived form, for the striking is not present in "ḍāraba" and "ḍaraba." If you say: The verbal noun is an independent word by which its meaning can be expressed, unlike the pattern, I say: The past-tense word is also like that, so there is no difference between the two: we borrow the explicit meaning of the verb word through the implicit meaning of it. It is not far-fetched that such a thing be called metaphor by transference, and the matter of naming is trivial and of no account. Perhaps they made the metaphor in such cases through the verbal noun and considered the notional difference, and did not consider what we have considered, namely the likening of time itself to time, such that the metaphor in the verb becomes by transference without strain, observing the principle of folding and unfolding as far as possible. Also, in whether the form and the pattern are part of the word, consider. Also, the pattern is not an independent part like the verbal noun. Also, the pattern is not a word, and metaphor is a division of the word. Perhaps the people did not turn their attention to these points, or some of them. End of quotation. There is discussion in this.

Al-Fadil Mir Sadr al-Din has a treatise on this noble verse, in which he dealt with the verifier's view on this point. Al-Fadil Yusuf al-Qarabaghi answered it with a treatise in which he extended the discussion, weighed and evaluated, and mentioned a number of possibilities regarding metaphor by transference. He inclined to the view that the pattern is a word, citing what he quoted from the commentary on the Mukhtasar of al-Adudi and from the commentary on the commentary by al-Taftazani, and supported it with other quotations. So let that be consulted, for although there is some scrutiny in part of it, it is not devoid of benefit.

The view that appears most probable to me is that the form (al-hay'a, the structure of the expression) is not itself a word, but it has the ruling of a word, and that it may be treated figuratively (tajawwuz), as with the informative statement (khabar) when it is used in the performative (inshā'). Also, the *majāz mursal* (metonymy, a figure based on a loose relation) is to be treated as *tabaʿiyya* (a dependent figure), on the basis of what they stated regarding the aspect of dependency in *isti'āra* (metaphor). As for al-Sadr's (Ibn al-Sadr) distinction, namely that the relation (ʿalāqa) in metaphor is considered at the moment of use, for they explicitly stated that the name of the comparandum (mushabbah bihi) is not applied to the compared (mushabbah) except after the latter has entered the genus of the comparandum, unlike *mursal*, where the relation merely prompts the transition and is not considered at the time of use. So there is no necessity to hold that it is dependent in this case. If that is established, it is of no benefit. Understand this.

Some have claimed that the past tense here is in its literal sense, on the basis that *al-fatḥ* (the opening, conquest) is a metaphor for facilitating and making it easy, and this does not depend on the conquest having occurred, so that it would be future relative to the time of revelation. Consider Moses, peace be upon him, who asked his Lord, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿And ease for me my affair﴾ (20:26), that He make his affair easy, namely his caliphate on earth and what accompanies it. He was granted this at the moment of the request, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You have been given your request, O Moses﴾ (20:36), though he had not yet undertaken anything. To interpret it as a promise to give the request is contrary to the apparent meaning. You know that what the majority adopted is more apparent and more eloquent. In the use of the future in the form of the past, to treat it as if it were certain, there is a grandeur and an indication of the exalted status of the one who speaks, which is not hidden, as in the *Kashshāf* (al-Zamakhshari). This, it is said, is because it indicates that all times are equal in His sight, Exalted is He, and that the one awaited is like one already realized; and that when He, glorified is He, wills a matter, it is certainly realized; and that because of the majesty of His status, when He reports an event, it is as though it exists, given its near and distant causes. Other views have also been stated.

The matter of the past tense in the speech of God, Exalted is He, has been raised as a problem, on the basis of the affirmation of the eternal inner speech (al-kalām al-nafsī al-azalī), since it would entail falsehood, because the truth of a statement requires that the relation has previously occurred, and precedence over eternity cannot be conceived. It has been answered that His eternal inner speech, Exalted is He, is not characterized by past or other tenses, because there is no time there. It has been objected that realizing this, along with the view that the eternal is the signified of the verbal speech, is extremely difficult; and likewise the view that what is characterized by the past or other tenses is only the originated word, not the eternal meaning. Some have answered that the difficulty would arise if the indication of the verbal speech on it were the indication of the signifier on the signified, but this is not so according to them; rather it is the indication of the effect on the cause. Taking something into account in the effect does not require taking it into account in the cause. It is not hidden, however, that the indication being that of the effect on the cause is contrary to the apparent meaning. Ibn al-Sadr said regarding this: the inclusion of past, present and future in verbal speech is with regard to the time of the addressee, not the time of the speaker, as when you send Zayd to ʿAmr and in your letter to him you write: "I have sent Zayd to you," even though at the time you write it the sending has not yet been realized. So you take into account the state of the addressee. And as when you imagine an addressee in yourself and say: "You did not do such-and-such just now, and before that he did such-and-such." Undoubtedly, this past, present and future is relative to the time of the existence of this imagined addressee, not relative to the time of the speaker of the inner speech, because he is directed to an imagined addressee, in whom only the times of the imagined addressees are considered. What the grammarians of Arabic have taken into account, namely the narration of a past state and the consideration of past, present and future in the circumstantial clause (al-jumla al-ḥāliyya) relative to the time of the verb and not the time of speaking, is very close to this. The end of his words. The verifier Mirzajan has a discussion on this point, which may be sought in his glosses on the commentary of al-ʿAḍud (al-Iji's commentary on the Mukhtasar).

It has been said: the intended "conquest" (al-fatḥ) is the conquest of the Romans, the genitive being the object of the verb, for they were overcome by the Persians in the year of the revelation. That it was a conquest for him, upon him be peace and blessings, is because he reported the unseen, and what he reported came true in that year; and because he took it as an omen (tafāʾul), since the People of the Book, who were believers, would prevail. In that is the manifestation of his affair, peace and blessings of God be upon him, which is equivalent to a conquest. It has been said: therefore there is a metaphor in "conquest," likening the manifestation of his affair, peace and blessings of God be upon him, to conquest. It has been said: there is no metaphor in it; the figurative element lies only in its being connected to him, upon him be peace and blessings. It has been said: there is no metaphor at all, and the meaning is: We conquered over the Romans for your sake.

You know that taking *al-fatḥ* in the sense he mentioned is very remote.

It has been objected against this that the conquest of the Romans was not caused by jihad or the like, so what they stated regarding the justification of the following causal clause cannot stand. It is reported from Qatada that *fataḥnā* is from *al-futāḥa* with a *ḍamma*, which means judgment, i.e., "We have decided for you against the people of Mecca that you and your companions shall enter it next year to circumambulate the House." This too is remote. It has been said: the intended meaning is that God, Exalted is He, opened for him, upon him be peace and blessings, through Islam, prophethood, and the call with proof and the sword. Close to this is what al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) transmitted, that He, Mighty and Majestic, opened for him, upon him be peace and blessings, through knowledge and guidance, which are means to reward and praiseworthy stations. Its remoteness is as previously mentioned. In any case, the omission of the object is for the purpose of focusing on the act itself, and to indicate that the criterion of the good tidings is the conquest itself, proceeding from Him, glorified is He, not the particularity of what is conquered. The placing of *laka* (for you) before the absolute object, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a manifest conquest﴾, although the original order is to place it before the other objects, as the scholar al-Taftazani explicitly stated, is for the sake of emphasis on the fact that this is for his benefit, upon him be peace and blessings. It has been said: because it is the axis of the benefit. And *mubīn* (manifest) is from *abāna*, in the sense of the intransitive *bāna*, meaning: a conquest that is clear, its matter evident and its state uncovered, or one that distinguishes between truth and falsehood.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 2:**

﴿That Allah may forgive you﴾. The position of the Ash'arites (al-Ash'ariyya), who hold that the acts of the Exalted are not caused by purposes ('illal bil-aghrad), is that this kind of lam (lam al-'aqibah, the lam of consequence) either denotes consequence, or likens what follows it to the final cause (al-'illah al-ghā'iyyah, the final cause) in the sense that the matter depends on what it is attached to. The forgiveness is consequent upon the conquest, because in it there is striving on his part (ﷺ) to elevate the word of Allah the Exalted, by enduring the hardships of war and plunging into the sources of calamities. The early generations (al-salaf), as Ibn al-Qayyim and others said, hold that the acts of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are caused by purposes. In Sharh al-Maqasid by the scholar al-Taftazani, it is stated that among the arguments of the Ash'arites, and of those who agree with them on this claim, is what indicates that they intended the universality of negation (umum al-salb), and among their arguments is what indicates that they intended the negation of universality (salb al-'umum). He then said: The truth is that some of the acts of the Exalted are caused by wisdoms and benefits, and that is evident, and the texts bear witness to it. As for generalising this, that no act of His, glory be to Him, is free of a purpose, that is a matter for discussion. Al-Isfahani, in his commentary on al-Tawali', mentioned in this question a disagreement with the Mu'tazila and most of the jurists. I say: I follow what the early generations held, because causation (al-ta'lil) exists in more than ten thousand verses and hadiths, and insisting on interpreting all of them is a departure from fairness. What those present cite as evidence is refuted with the slightest reflection, as is not hidden from one who has studied the books of the early scholars, may God have mercy on them. In al-Kashshaf, [al-Zamakhshari] did not make the conquest a cause of the forgiveness, but [made the whole] due to the combination of the four matters he enumerated: the forgiveness, the completion of the blessing, the guidance to the straight path, and the mighty victory, as if it were said: We facilitated for you the conquest of Makkah and gave you victory over your enemy, so that We might combine for you the honour of both abodes and the aims of the immediate and the deferred. Its summary, as the scholar said, is that the conquest was not made a cause for each of the items conjoined after the lam, namely the forgiveness, the completion of the blessing, the guidance, and the victory, but rather for their combination. It suffices in this that it has a share in the attainment of some of them, such as the completion of the blessing and the mighty victory. Its verification, as he said, is that the conjunction upon what is governed by the lam may be for sharing in the object of the lam, as in: "I came to you so that I may win your meeting and obtain your gifts"; it may be like repeating the lam and conjoining one prepositional phrase to another; and it may be for sharing in the meaning of the lam, as in: "I came to you so that you may settle in your position and pour upon me of your bounty", that is, for the combination of the two matters; and it may be of the type of: "The servant of Zayd and 'Amr came to me", meaning the servant who belongs to both of them. It has been put forward, to avert the suspicion that if the intended thing is a part, then mentioning the rest is superfluous, that: each of the two is either intended in itself, and this is evident, or the intended thing is a part, and in that case mentioning the other is either because it depends on it, or because its connection to it is strong, or because it follows from it; so it is mentioned to indicate that the two are like one thing, as in His saying: ﴿So that if one of them errs, the other will remind her﴾, and your saying: "I have prepared the wood so that the wall may lean, and so I shall prop it up, and I have kept close to my creditor so that I may collect my right and release him." The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words is that what is intended in our case is only to give the reason for the collective condition, so reflect in order to know which of these categories it belongs to. Know that what is well known is that the cause is what the lam enters upon, not what it is attached to, as is the apparent sense of the expression in al-Kashshaf. But it has been verified that when it enters upon the end-point (al-ghāyah), it is correct to say that what follows it is a cause, meaning in terms of rational conception; and it is correct to say that what it is attached to is a cause, meaning in terms of existence. So do not overlook this. The author of al-Ghaniyyan claimed that the lam here is the lam of oath, and that it was given a kasra and the nun was dropped from the verb, by analogy with the lam of kay. It was refuted on the ground that the lam of oath is not given a kasra, nor does it govern the subjunctive, for it has not been heard in [the phrase] "By God, Zayd will stand", meaning "Zayd will surely stand". He defended himself by saying that the kasra has been explained by its resemblance to the lam of kay.

As for the nasb (the subjunctive), he may say concerning it: it is not a nasb at all, but rather the vowel that accompanies the presence of the nun, which remained after its deletion as an indication of the deletion. You know that this is of no benefit in the absence of transmission. Furthermore, the turning to the proper name (ism al-dhat), which implies all the attributes, has been said to serve to indicate that each of those matters included in the chain of the end-point among the acts of the Exalted proceeds from Him, Mighty and Majestic, from an aspect different from the aspect of the others, and is consequent upon one of His attributes, exalted is His majesty.

Al-Sadr said: It is not far-fetched to say that the expression of Him, exalted be He, in the context of forgiveness, by the majestic name which indicates the attributes of beauty and majesty, indicates that His forgiveness precedes His punishment. In al-Bahr: Since forgiveness and what follows it are shared in their application, the Messenger (ﷺ) and others use them, as in His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾, and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you﴾, and His saying: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾, and His saying, Mighty and Majestic: (He guides whom He wills), and His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿Indeed, they are the ones who will be victorious﴾. Since the conquest was specific to the Messenger (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him), He attributed it to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah), magnifying his station, and He attributed those other things to the apparent noun and its pronoun, [which is] as you see, even though al-Imam (al-Razi) also said it. I say: It is possible that in attributing the forgiveness to Him, exalted be He, by the greatest name, after attributing the conquest to Him by the plural of majesty, there is an allusion that the forgiveness is among the things which He, glory be to Him, takes charge of Himself, whereas the conquest is among the things which He, exalted be His majesty, takes charge of through intermediaries. Some have stated that the custom of great persons is to refer to themselves with the first-person plural form, because what proceeds from them is for the most part carried out through their servants. It is not objected that victory, like conquest, was attributed to the majestic name, for reasons which are not hidden from you. The fronting of ﴿for you﴾ before the direct object, namely His saying: ﴿what has preceded of your sin and what has followed﴾, is for the reason already mentioned more than once. "Ma" (what) is for generality, and "al-mutaqaddim" (what has preceded) and "al-muta'akhkhir" (what has followed) are for comprehensiveness, as a metonymy for the whole. What is meant by sin (dhanb) is what has been committed of that which is contrary to the better course (khilaf al-awla), relative to his station, upon him be prayers and peace; so it belongs to the category of "the good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near". It may also be said: what is meant is what is a sin in the eyes of his lofty view (ﷺ), even though it is not a sin nor contrary to the better course in the sight of Allah, the Exalted, as the idafah (construct) hints at.

Al-Sadr said: It is possible that His saying, exalted be He: ("That He may forgive") and so on, is a metonymy for the absence of censure, or of the category of the figurative metaphor (al-isti'arah al-tamthiliyyah), without the realisation of the meanings of the individual words. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Amir and Abu Ja'far that they said: "What preceded" refers to [his sins] in the Jahiliyyah, and "what followed" refers to [his sins] in Islam. It was also said: "What preceded" refers to the story of Mariyah, and "what followed" refers to the wife of Zayd, but this is nothing [of substance], though the reverse would be more appropriate, since the story of Zayd's wife came earlier. In the verse, together with what is known of his (ﷺ) condition of great worship, there is that which indicates the nobility of his station to a degree that no expression can encompass. And it is authentically related that "when this was revealed, he (ﷺ) fasted and prayed until his feet swelled, and he devoted himself to worship until he became like a worn-out waterskin. It was said to him: Do you do this to yourself, when Allah has forgiven you what preceded of your sin and what followed? He, upon him be prayers and peace, said: Should I not be a grateful servant?"

﴿And complete His favour upon you﴾, by the elevation of the religion and its spread in the lands, and other things which Allah, exalted be He, has bestowed upon him (ﷺ) of blessings, religious and worldly; ﴿and guide you to a straight path﴾, in conveying the message and establishing the prescribed punishments. It has been said: although the basis of uprightness was already present before the conquest, there was attained after it, through the clarification of the paths of truth and the uprightness of its methods, what had not been attained before.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 3:

﴿And God will help you﴾. The explicit mention of the Majestic Name (al-Jalalah) along with the help is for the following reason. It has been said that it is because it is the final (ultimate) cause (khatimat al-'ilal, the concluding cause) or the final aim (ghayat, end-goal). It is also to show the complete care for his (the Prophet's) status, as indicated by its being followed by His words, may He be exalted: ﴿a mighty help﴾. Al-Sadr said: "He made the Name explicit in the earlier verse and here because forgiveness relates to the Hereafter, while help relates to this world. So it is as if it was indicated, by attributing forgiveness and help to the explicit Name of God, that God, mighty and majestic, is the One who takes charge of your affairs in this world and the Hereafter." The Imam said:

"The Majesty (al-Jalalah) was made explicit here to indicate that help can only come from God, may He be exalted, as He said: ﴿And there is no help except from God﴾. This is because help comes through patience, and patience comes through God, as He said: ﴿And your patience is only through God﴾, because it is the tranquillity of the heart and its being at rest, and that comes through the remembrance of God: ﴿Surely by the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾."

The "mighty" (al-'Aziz), according to the apparent meaning, refers to the one who is helped (al-mansur). Where it is ascribed to help (nasr), it is either in the sense of attribution (lil-nisbah), although the known form for that is the active participle such as لابن (possessor of milk) and the intensive form such as بزّاز (cloth merchant), meaning a help in which there is might and protection (mana'ah); or it is a figurative attribution (tajawwuz fi al-isnad) in the manner of describing the verbal noun with the passive form, and here the one meant is the one helped, as in ( عذاب ألِيم ) (a painful punishment) according to one opinion, not the helper (al-nasir). This is because it has been said that it does not fit the context and its benefit is little, since the discussion concerns the status of the one addressed who is helped, not the speaker who helps. Yet there is something in this. It has also been said: the statement contains an implied genitive construction (taqdir mudaf), meaning "its possessor is mighty," and that one is the one helped. But this involves the strain of deletion and connection.

It may be said: it needs something of what has been mentioned, since there is no obstacle to describing help as mighty, as is the apparent meaning, based on one of the meanings of "might" ('izzah), which is rarity of existence and difficulty of attainment. The meaning is: God will help you with a help whose like is rare to exist and difficult to attain. Al-Raghib has said this regarding His words: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty Book﴾. I found this to be the view of al-Sadr after I had copied it from his writing. So reflect, and do not be one who is incapable.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 4:

﴿It is He who sent down tranquility (al-sakinah) into the hearts of the believers﴾. This explains what He, glorified is He, bestowed upon them of the beginnings of the victory. By al-sakinah is meant tranquility and steadfastness, derived from sukun (rest), that is, He sent it into their hearts through the peace and security, to show His favor toward them by facilitating security after fear. By "sending it down" is meant creating and bringing it into existence. The expression "sending down" implies the exalted status of this tranquility.

Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: God's sending down of His blessing upon a servant is His giving it to him, and this is either by sending down the thing itself, as with the sending down of the Qur'an, or by sending down its causes and guidance toward it, as with the sending down of iron and the like. It has also been said that anzala (to send down) comes from nazala (to alight) in a place, meaning he set down his baggage there, and anzalahu (he caused him to alight) is the causative form. So the meaning is that He settled tranquility in their hearts, and their hearts became a dwelling place and a refuge for it. It has also been said that al-sakinah is an angel who dwells in the heart of the believer and gives him security, as it is narrated that ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him and ennoble his face, said: "Indeed, al-sakinah speaks upon the tongue of ʿUmar." The matter of its being sent down upon him is very evident.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and others, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: al-sakinah is mercy. It has also been said: it is intellect, and it is called sakinah when one is at rest from inclination toward desires and from terror. It has also been said: it is gravity and majesty for Allah, exalted is He, and for His Messenger (ﷺ). It has also been said: it derives from sakana ila kadha (he was inclined to such-and-such), meaning He sent into their hearts the stillness and inclination toward what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought of the sacred laws. The most preponderant of the interpretations here, according to al-Khafaji, is the first. As for what some have mentioned, that al-sakinah is a thing that has a head like the head of a cat, I do not see this as a valid statement.

﴿So that they might increase in faith (iman) along with their faith﴾, that is, certainty along with their certainty, through the firm establishment of belief and the tranquility of souls upon it. Since faith was established across the times, the renewal of its times was treated as the renewal and increase of it, so this was borrowed for it and was given the hint by the word "along with" (maʿa). It has also been said: the increase of faith is by the increase of what one believes in. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the first thing the Prophet (ﷺ) brought them was tawhid (the oneness of God), then prayer and almsgiving, then pilgrimage and jihad, so they increased in faith along with their faith. As for whoever says that actions are part of faith, he says that faith itself, that is, faith composed of these and other things, increases and decreases, and he did not need to interpret the verse but made it evidence for his view.

The detailed discussion on this subject is that the majority of the Ash'aris, al-Qalanisi, the jurists, the traditionists, and the Mu'tazilah held that faith increases and decreases, and this was attributed to al-Shafi'i and Malik. Al-Bukhari said: "I met more than a thousand scholars in the cities, and I did not see any of them differ that faith is speech and action, and that it increases and decreases." They argued for this by reason and by transmission. As for the first, if the reality of faith did not vary, then the faith of the ordinary members of the community who are immersed in corruption and sins would be equal to the faith of the prophets, peace be upon them, for example, and the consequence is false, so the antecedent is false. As for the second, it is due to the abundance of texts on this meaning, among them the verse mentioned, and among them what is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "We said: O Messenger of Allah, faith increases and decreases. He said: Yes, it increases until it brings its companion into Paradise, and it decreases until it brings its companion into the Fire."

And among them what is narrated from ʿUmar and Jabir, may Allah be pleased with both of them, as a raised report: "If the faith of Abu Bakr were weighed against the faith of this entire community, it would outweigh it."

It was objected that the non-acceptance of increase and decrease, if the acts of obedience are included in its meaning, is more fitting and more deserving than its non-acceptance of that when its meaning is only tasdiq (affirmation by the heart).

First, because there is no rank above all deeds for it to be an increase, nor a faith below it for it to be a decrease. Second, because no one could then attain complete faith, and increase over what has not yet been completed is impossible. It was answered that this applies only to the Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij, who hold that faith is negated by the negation of any of the deeds, whereas the majority only say that they are a condition of perfection in faith, so the absence of them entails only the absence of perfection, which does not undermine the basis of faith.

Al-Nawawi and a group of verifying scholars of kalam (scholastic theology) said: faith in the sense of inner affirmation (al-tasdiq al-qalbi) also increases and decreases, through the increase of reflection and the clarity of proofs and their absence. For this reason the faith of the saints (al-siddiqin) is stronger than the faith of others, to the extent that doubts do not assail it. This is supported by the fact that each person knows that what is in his heart varies, so that at some times he is greater in certainty and sincerity than at others. Likewise, tasdiq and knowledge vary according to the clarity and abundance of proofs. It was objected that if this is accepted, it would be doubt. It was answered that the degrees of certainty vary, up to knowledge of certainty (ʿilm al-yaqin), truth of certainty (haqq al-yaqin), and eye of certainty (ʿayn al-yaqin), although no doubt accompanies them. Among those who agreed with al-Nawawi in what he affirmed is al-Sa'd (al-Taftazani) in the second section of his Tahdhib. A group of scholars, the greatest of whom is Imam Abu Hanifa, and his followers and many of the theologians, said: faith neither increases nor decreases. Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) chose this view. They argued that it is the name of affirmation that reaches the limit of certainty and firm assent, and in this there is no conceivable increase or decrease. So the affirmer, when he adds acts of obedience to it or commits sins, his affirmation has not changed at all in its basis. It only varies if it is the name of acts of obedience, which vary in quantity and quality. They answered what the earlier scholars relied upon with several arguments, among them what we indicated first, that the increase is according to continuance, steadiness, and the abundance of times and periods. Its clarification is what Imam al-Haramayn said:

The Prophet (ﷺ) surpasses others by the continuity of his affirmation and by Allah's protection of him from the intrusion of doubts. Affirmation is an accident that does not remain in its individual instance but is renewed through its like, so the Prophet, peace be upon him, has successive instances of it, while for others they occur only in intervals. Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) has numbers of faith that are established for him, and only some of them are established for others, so his faith (ﷺ) is greater. Increase in this sense is said to be beyond dispute.

It was objected that the occurrence of a like after the cessation of a thing is not an increase in it, like the blackness of a body. It was answered that what is meant is the increase of instances that have occurred, and that non-persistence does not contradict this. Another argument is what we indicated second, that the increase is according to the increase of what one believes in. The Companions, may the pleasure of Allah be upon all of them, first believed in what they believed in, and the sacred law was not yet complete, and rulings were descending little by little, so they believed in each of them as it was renewed. There is no doubt that people's faith varies by considering the details, in quantity and quality, and this is not restricted to his time (ﷺ), since the details could be known in other ages as well. Another argument is that what is meant is the increase of its fruit and the radiance of its light in the heart, for the light of faith increases through acts of obedience and decreases through sins. It was said: this is needed only after establishing a decisive proof that affirmation cannot accept increase and decrease, and if no decisive proof has been established for that, the more fitting course is to leave the apparent meanings as they are.

Al-Khattabi said: faith is speech, and it neither increases nor decreases; it is action, and it increases and decreases; it is belief, and it increases and does not decrease, so if it decreases it is gone. It was objected that if it increases and then returns to what it was, it has decreased but has not gone. It was answered that his meaning is that belief, in terms of its first degree, increases and does not decrease, not that belief absolutely is like this. A group, among them Imam al-Razi and Imam al-Haramayn, held that the disagreement is verbal, by taking the statement of negation to refer to the basis of faith, which is tasdiq, so it neither increases nor decreases, and taking the statement of affirmation to refer to what completes it, which is the deeds. Thus the disagreement on this question becomes a branch of the disagreement over the definition of faith. The truth is that the disagreement is real, because of what you have heard from Imam al-Nawawi and those with him, that tasdiq itself increases and decreases.

Some verifying scholars said: increase and decrease are properties of what is judged (al-hukm), and tasdiq is a kind of knowledge, and no one has said that it belongs to the category of quantity (kam). It has been said rather that it is a quality (kayf), or an affection (infi'al), or a relation and connection between the knower and the known, or a quality with relation. The most famous view is that it is a quality (kayf). So when this is valid, and we hold that intensity and weakness differ from increase and decrease, there is no harm in understanding them in the texts and other places as intensity and weakness, and this is a well-known metaphor. Denying that faith is described by them comes close to obstinacy, so consider this carefully. Some have mentioned here that the faith which is the object of the word "huwa" (it is) is natural faith (al-iman al-fitri), and the faith mentioned before it is inferential faith (al-iman al-istidlali), so it is as if it were said: "so that they might increase in inferential faith along with their natural faith." There is in this as much obscurity as there is.

﴿And to Allah belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth﴾: He manages their affairs however He wills. He sets some of them over others at times, and He, glorified is He, brings peace among them at other times, according to what His will requires, which is founded on wisdoms and interests. Among the consequences of this is what occurred at Hudaybiyyah. ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾, exceedingly so in knowledge of all matters, ﴿Wise﴾ in His decree and His management, mighty and majestic is He.
