And His saying, may He be glorified, ﴿that He may admit the believing men and the believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾ is connected to what is implied by the mention that the hosts of the heavens and the earth belong to Him, may His majesty be exalted, in the sense of disposal and management (tasarruf wa tadbir). Some eminent scholars have stated that this is a metonymy (kinaya) for Him, meaning: God, glorified is He, arranged what He arranged of empowering the believers so that they would recognise God's blessing in that and be thankful for it, and so He would admit them into Paradise. Thus the real reason is the recognition of the blessing and giving thanks for it. But since it was the cause of entering Paradise, the effect (musabbab) was put in the place of the cause (sabab). It was also said that it is connected to "fataḥna" (We gave you a victory), and it was said to be connected to "anzala" (He sent down). Its connection to that, along with the connection of the other lam to it, is based on the first being connected to it unrestrictedly and the second restrictedly. The difference between the two descriptions is treated as a difference between two persons, for otherwise two prepositional phrases with the same meaning cannot be attached to one governing word without a conjunction. It was said to be connected to "yanṣuraka" (He will help you), and said to be connected to "yazdāda" (He may increase), and said to be connected to all that has been mentioned, either by way of tanāzu' (competition between two governing words for one complement) with its estimate, or by estimating something that includes that, such as: "He, glorified is He, did what was mentioned so that He might admit..." etc. It was also said that it is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition) of "li-yazdāda" (so that they may increase), for admitting the believing men and believing women into Paradise, and likewise what is conjoined to it, entails an increase in faith. Badal al-ishtimal depends on a connection between the substituted and the substituted-from such that one of them suggests the other, without being totality or partiality. Perhaps the more evident is the first view. The mention of the believing women here alongside the believing men is to preclude the assumption that the ruling is restricted to men, because of jihad and the conquest being at their hands. Likewise, in every passage that might suggest restriction, women are explicitly mentioned. Something similar will be said later. Thus it has been said.

Ibn Jarir and a group [of narrators] related from Anas, who said: "It was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿That God may forgive you your former and latter sins﴾ on his return from al-Hudaybiyah. He said: 'There has been revealed to me a verse more beloved to me than everything on earth.' Then he recited it to them. They said: 'Congratulations, O Messenger of God! God has explained to you what He will do with you; so what will He do with us?' Then it was revealed: ﴿that He may admit the believing men and the believing women﴾ up to ﴿a great victory﴾."

﴿And that He may remove from them their misdeeds﴾, that is, He covers them and does not expose them. The intended meaning is that He erases them, glorified is He, and does not call them to account for them. The placing of admission before expiation in the mention, although in existence the order is the reverse, is for the sake of hastening to state what is the aim. This is what more than one has said. In my view it is also permissible that the expiation be in Paradise, so that the meaning is: He admits them to Paradise and covers their misdeeds and conceals them from them, so they never pass through their minds, and they do not mention them at all, lest they feel shame and the clarity of their life be troubled. Something similar has passed.

﴿And that was, with God, a great victory﴾, that is, what has been mentioned of admission and expiation, is ﴿a victory whose worth cannot be measured﴾, because it is the ultimate of what high aspirations stretch their necks toward, of bringing benefit and repelling harm. "With God" (ʿinda Allāh) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of "fawzan" (a victory), because when the description of an indefinite noun is placed before it, it is parsed as a ḥāl. That it may be a ḥāl when placed after "ʿaẓīman" (great) is no problem, contrary to what has been imagined; that is, existing with God, i.e., in His knowledge and decree, glorified is He, and the clause is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) that confirms what precedes it.

[Page 95]

The statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿and that He may punish the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and the polytheist women﴾, is coordinated (ʿatf) with "that He may admit" (yudkhila), meaning: "and that He may punish the hypocrite men, etc., in order to enrage them by that." This is evident according to all the aforementioned interpretations of ﴿that He may admit﴾, including the interpretation of substitution (badal), since inclusive substitution (badal al-ishtimal) is validated by association (mulabasa), as has passed. The increase in faith, according to what we mentioned in its explanation, is undoubtedly something that enrages them. It has been said that on this interpretation it is a coordination with the substituted element (al-mubdal minhu). The mention of the hypocrites before the polytheists is because they are more harmful to the Muslims, so hastening their punishment brings joy.

﴿those who harbour an evil thought about Allah﴾, that is, an evil, blameworthy opinion, namely that He, Mighty and Majestic, does not support His Messenger ﷺ and the believers. It has been said that what is meant is what encompasses that and all their other corrupt opinions, such as polytheism or other things. ﴿Upon them is a turn of evil﴾, that is, what they assume and lie in wait for against the believers returns upon them; it encircles them and turns back upon them. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read (dāʾirat al-suʾ) with a ḍamma. The difference between it and (al-suʾ) with a fatḥa, according to what is in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, is that the one with fatḥa is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the one with ḍamma is a noun of the verbal noun (ism al-maṣdar), meaning harm.

Others have said: "They are two dialects with the same meaning, like al-kurh and al-karh according to al-Kisāʾī." Both are originally verbal nouns, except that the one with fatḥa became common when followed by what is intended to be censured, while the one with ḍamma took the course of evil. Since the "turn" here is praiseworthy and is attributed to the one with fatḥa in the reading of the majority, it is necessary according to this view to say that it is interpreted as blameworthy in relation to those upon whom it turns, namely the hypocrites and polytheists. Its use for what is disliked is more common, and it is a verbal noun in the pattern of an active participle or an active participle itself. Its construction, according to al-Ṭībī, is the attribution of the qualified to the qualifier for emphasis (mubālagha). In al-Kashshāf, the attribution is in the sense of "min" as in "dāʾirat dhahab," so reflect upon this.

The statement is either a report of the occurrence of evil upon them or a supplication against them. The statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿and Allah has become angry with them and has cursed them and prepared for them Hell﴾, is coordinated with that. The apparent wording would have been "fa-laʿanahum fa-aʿadda" with fāʾ in both places, but He deviated from it to indicate that each of the two matters is independent in the threat, without considering causation in it. ﴿And evil is the destination﴾, namely Hell.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 7:

﴿And to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth.﴾ It was mentioned earlier that the intended meaning is that He, may He be exalted and glorified, is the one who manages the affairs of the created beings in accordance with His wisdom; therefore it was followed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Knowing, Wise.﴾ Here, however, it is intended as a warning that they are within the grip of the power of the Avenger; therefore it was followed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is ever Mighty and Wise.﴾ So there is no repetition, as al-Shihab (al-Alusi's reference to al-Khafaji, Shihab al-Din) has said. It was also said: the soldiers are soldiers of mercy and soldiers of punishment, and the intended meaning here is the second, as indicated by the mention of the attribute of might.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾ i.e., over your ummah, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [2:143]. And ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah: "a witness over your ummah, and a witness over the prophets, peace be upon them, that they have conveyed (the message)." ﴿And a bringer of good tidings﴾ of reward for obedience, ﴿and a warner﴾ of punishment for disobedience.

[p. 96]

﴿That you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ and his community, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾. This is from the device of *taghlib* (giving precedence to one party within a combined address), in which the addressed party is given precedence over the absent party. It thus conveys that the Prophet, peace be upon him, is addressed to believe in his own message just as the community is, and this is indeed the case. Al-Wahidi said: the address in ﴿We have sent you﴾ is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the address in ﴿that you may believe﴾ is to his community. On this view, if the *lam* is causal (*lam al-ta'lil*), the thing caused is omitted, meaning: that you may believe in Allah, and such-and-such that the sending accomplished this. Or the *lam* is imperative, following the pattern of ﴿So let them rejoice in that﴾ according to the reading with the upper *ta'* (the second person). It is said that it means: say to them, "That you may believe," and so on. It is also said that it is addressed to the community, on the basis that the address to him ﷺ is treated as standing in the place of their address, so that it is in effect identical to it by claim (*idda'*). The *lam* is connected to "We have sent." This is not objected to by what al-Radi and others established, that it is impossible for two parties to be addressed in a single utterance without conjunction, dual or plural marking, because after the revelation there is no plurality. It has also been permitted that this is because they are, at that time, not addressed in reality, so their address is in the status of the third person. It is also said that the prohibition mentioned is conditional upon each of the addressed parties being independent. As for when one of them is included within the address of the other by his message, there is no prohibition, as is known from surveying their speech. In that case it is permissible for the address to the community to be intended as well, without *taghlib*. The discussion of this is lengthy, but what has been mentioned earlier is free of disputation and argument.

﴿And that you may support him﴾, that is, that you may help him, as is narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, traced to the Prophet (*marfu'*), and as a group transmitted it from Qatadah. The pronoun refers to Allah, mighty and majestic, and His support, glorified is He, is by supporting His religion and His Messenger ﷺ. ﴿And honour him﴾, that is, that you may magnify him, as Qatadah and others said. The pronoun also refers to Him, exalted is He. It is said that both pronouns refer to the Messenger ﷺ, and this is narrated from Ibn Abbas. Some claimed that it is necessarily the case that the pronoun in ﴿support him﴾ refers to the Messenger, peace be upon him, out of a supposed notion that *ta'zir* cannot be directed to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, just as it is agreed by all that the pronoun in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and glorify Him﴾ refers to Allah, glorified is He. It is not hidden that the better view is that the two pronouns in what preceded also refer to Allah, exalted is He, so as to avoid disjoining the pronouns without necessity (*fakk al-damair*), that is: and that you may glorify Allah, exalted is He, or pray to Him, glorified is He, from *al-subha* (glorification). ﴿Morning and evening﴾, that is, at dawn and at dusk. The intended meaning is their apparent sense, or the whole of the day, and a whole thing is referred to by its two extremes, as one says "east and west" to mean the whole world. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it means the Fajr prayer, the Zuhr prayer, and the Asr prayer.

Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywah, Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr recited the four verbs, namely *li-tu'minu* and what follows it, with the third-person plural *ya'* (the verbs being in the absent form). It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Jubayr likewise, except that the two of them read ﴿and glorify Allah﴾ with the Name of Majesty in place of the pronoun. Al-Jahdari read *ta'zuruhu* with a *ta'* (upper) vowelled with fatha and a *zay* vowelled with damma, lightly stressed (*mukhaffafan*). In another narration from him, the *ta'* is vowelled with fatha and the *zay* with kasra, lightly stressed. This is also narrated from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

It has also been read with the *ta'* vowelled with damma and the *zay* with kasra, lightly stressed. Ibn Abbas and Muhammad ibn al-Yamani read *tu'azzizuhu* with two *zay*s, from *al-izzah* (might), meaning: that you may make him mighty. This is in relation to Allah, glorified is He, by making His religion and His Messenger ﷺ mighty. It has also been read *wa-tuwaqqiruhu*, from *awqarahu*, with the same meaning as *waqqarahu*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you﴾ on the day of al-Hudaybiyah, [pledging] to die in your support, as narrated from Salamah ibn al-Akwa' and others; or [pledging] not to flee from Quraysh, as narrated from Ibn Umar and Jabir, may Allah be pleased with them. The discussion of the details of this will come, if Allah the Exalted wills. The pledge (al-mubaya'ah) took place before the revelation of the verse, so the use of the present tense is to bring the past situation to mind. It is a form of mufa'alah from al-bay' (sale). One says: "baya'a al-sultan mubaya'atan" when he commits himself thereby to obedience to him in exchange for what he gives him (radakha lahu), and it is often used of the well-known pledge of allegiance to sultans and the like, even if he did not give anything. As for what occurred with the believers, it is said that it alludes to what is in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives﴾, the verse, ﴿They only pledge allegiance to Allah﴾, because the aim of the pledge to the Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, and obedience to him, is obedience to Allah the Exalted and compliance with His commands, glorified is He, according to His saying the Exalted: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾. So the pledging to Allah the Exalted in the sense of obeying Him, glorified is He, is a figure of speech by association (mushakalah), or it is pure metaphor (majaz). It was also read as (innama yubayi'una lillah), meaning for the sake of Allah and for His countenance, and the object is omitted, i.e., "they only pledge allegiance to you for Allah's sake." ﴿The hand of Allah is over their hands﴾: this is a resumptive sentence that emphasizes what precedes it, because it is an expression for the pledge. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: when He, glorified is He, said: ﴿They only pledge allegiance to Allah﴾, He emphasized it in the manner of imagery (takhyil), saying: ﴿The hand of Allah is over their hands﴾, and He, glorified is He, is exalted above limbs and the attributes of bodies; the meaning is only the affirmation that the binding of the covenant with the Messenger ﷺ is like His binding with Allah the Exalted, without any difference between them. In al-Miftah: as for the excellence of the imaginative metaphor (al-isti'arah al-takhyiliyyah), it is according to the excellence of the metaphor by implication (al-isti'arah bil-kinayah) whenever it follows it, as in your saying: "So-and-so is between the fangs of death and its claws." Then, when the figure of association is added to it, as in (the hand of Allah) etc., it becomes better and better. He means that in the name of Allah the Exalted there is a metaphor by implication, likening Him, glorified and exalted is He, to the one who pledges allegiance, and "the hand" is an imaginative metaphor, together with the fact that there is also an association in its mention alongside the hands of people. The prohibition of metaphor in the name of Allah the Exalted applies only to the explicit metaphor (al-isti'arah al-tasrihiyyah), not the implicit one, because it does not entail applying His name to other than Him, glorified is He. Al-Wahidi narrated from Ibn Kaysan: "the hand" means power, i.e., the power of Allah the Exalted and His support is above their power and their support; that is, trust in the support of Allah the Exalted for you, not in their support, even if they pledge allegiance to you.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: the hand of Allah in fulfilling [the covenant] is above their hands, or in reward is above their hands in obedience, or the hand of Allah, glorified is He, in bestowing favor upon them through guidance is above their hands in obedience. It was said: the meaning is the blessing of Allah the Exalted upon them by enabling them to pledge allegiance to you is above their blessing, which is their pledge to you, and greater than it. There is in this something of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Do not consider your Islam a favor upon me; rather, Allah confers a favor upon you that He has guided you to faith﴾. All of these are interpretations that the later scholars (al-khalaf) have undertaken, and the best of them is what was mentioned first. The earlier scholars (al-salaf) pass the verse as it came, while affirming the exaltation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, above limbs and the attributes of bodies, and they do likewise in all the ambiguous verses (al-mutashabihat), saying: knowing the reality of that is a branch of knowing the reality of the Essence, and how could that be? Far, far away. It is also permitted that the sentence be a second predicate after the predicate of inna, and likewise it is permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (yubayi'unaka); and regarding the permissibility of that, given that it is a nominal sentence not connected with a waw, there is discussion.

﴿Whoever breaks [the oath]﴾ breaks the covenant, ﴿then he breaks only against himself﴾, so the harm of his breaking returns only upon him. Al-Zamakhshari narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah that no one broke the pledge except Jadd ibn Qays, and he was a hypocrite. But what al-Tibi narrated from Muslim indicates that the man did not pledge at all, rather than that he pledged and then broke it. He said: Jabir was asked, "How many were there on the day of al-Hudaybiyah?" He said: "We were fourteen hundred, and we pledged to him while Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, held his hand, under the tree, which was a samurah tree, and we pledged to him, except Jadd ibn Qays al-Ansari, who hid beneath the belly of his camel and did not go with the people." Perhaps this is the most consistent with the apparent meaning of His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you﴾.

Zayd ibn Ali read (yankithu) with a kasrah on the kaf. ﴿And whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with Allah, He will give him a great reward﴾: it is Paradise and what is in it of things that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that have not occurred to the heart of any human. It is said: "wafa bil-ahd" and "awfa bihi" when he completes it; awfa is the dialect of Tihamah, and from it is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Fulfill the contracts﴾.

﴿And those who fulfill their covenant﴾ was also read (bima 'ahada) in the triliteral form.

The majority read (alayhi) with a kasrah on the ha', as is common, while Hafs read it with a damma here. It was said: the reason for the damma is that it is the ha' of huwa and it is pronounced with damma, so that was carried over, as in lahu and daraba-hu; and the reason for the kasrah is to preserve the ya', and likewise in ilayhi and fihi, and likewise in cases where there is a kasrah before it, such as bihi and marartu bi-ghulamihi, because of the heaviness of moving from kasrah to damma. The damma in this verse is favored by the purpose of arriving at the magnification of the word Allah, which suits the magnification of the matter of the covenant that the discourse implies; and also, keeping what was as it was suits fulfilling the covenant, maintaining it, and not breaking it. I asked many of the eminent scholars, while I was still fresh in speaking, about the reason for this damma here, and I was not answered with anything that satisfied my heart; then I came upon what you have heard, and Allah the Exalted is the Guide to what is better than it.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn Amir, Rawh and Zayd ibn Ali read (fasanu'tihi) with the letter nun.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 11:

﴿The ones left behind from among the Bedouin will say to you﴾. Mujahid and others said, and the speech of some of them has entered into the speech of others: "The ones left behind from among the Bedouin" are Juhayna, Muzayna, Ghifar, Ashja', al-Dil and Aslam. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called upon them to go forth when he intended to set out for Makkah in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, performing 'umrah, so that they would accompany him, fearing that the Quraysh might confront him with war or bar him from the House. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) put on the ihram and drove the sacrificial animals with him, so that it would be known that he did not intend war. Those Bedouin saw that he (peace be upon him) was going to encounter a great number from the Quraysh, Thaqif, Kinana and the tribes neighbouring Makkah, namely the Ahabish, and faith had not yet taken firm root in their hearts. So they held back from the Prophet (ﷺ) and stayed behind, and they said: "We would go to a people who have attacked him in the heart of his home in Madina and killed his companions, so we would fight them?" And they said: "Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his companions will never return from this journey." So Allah exposed them in this verse, and informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of their words and their excuses before he reached them, and it happened exactly so.

"The ones left behind" (al-mukhallafun) is the plural of mukhallaf. Al-Tabarsi said: it is the one left behind in a place, after those who have departed from the town, derived from "khalf" (behind), whose opposite is "muqaddam" (ahead). "The Bedouin" (al-a'rab), according to the well-known usage, are the inhabitants of the desert among the Arabs, and it has no singular. That is: the ones left behind, those who did not go out with you, will say to you, offering excuses to you: ﴿Our possessions and our families have occupied us﴾ from going with you, ﴿for there was no one to attend to them and protect them from being lost﴾. Perhaps the mention of the families after the possessions is in the order of ascent, because guarding the family is more important to those possessed of jealousy than guarding possessions.

And Ibrahim ibn Nuh ibn Bazan read (shaghghalat) with a doubled ghayn, for intensification. ﴿So ask forgiveness for us﴾ from Allah, the Exalted, that He may forgive us our staying behind from you, since it was not out of laziness in your obedience, but because of that pressing concern. ﴿They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts﴾, meaning that their speech is from the tip of the tongue, not corresponding to what is in the hearts. This is a metonymy for their lying. The sentence is therefore a fresh statement refuting them, and it is not clearly a substitute for (will say). The lie relates to what the speech contains of the report about their staying behind, that it was due to a compelling necessity, namely the management of their affairs which must be done, and the absence of anyone to do it had they gone with him (peace be upon him). Likewise it relates to what the imperative (ask forgiveness) contains of their acknowledgement that they are sinners, and that his (peace be upon him) prayer for them would benefit them with a benefit that is binding on them. Or calling that a lie is not because of a mismatch between the relation of belief, as al-Nizam held, but because of its non-correspondence to reality according to their belief; and a distinction is made between the two matters.

﴿Say: Who then can hold anything for you against Allah, if He intends you harm or intends you benefit?﴾ This is a command to him (ﷺ) to answer them with this when they offer these falsehoods as excuses. Al-mulk is holding with strength, for it carries the meaning of control, and that is preservation through firmness. From it comes "I do not own the camel's halter" (la amliku ra's al-ba'ir), and "I owned the dough" (malaktu al-'ajin) when you tightened its kneading, and "I owned the thing" when it came fully under your control. When you say "I do not own" (la amliku), it is a negation of ability and capacity to hold and prevent. So the basic meaning here is: who then can hold for you any part of Allah's power, if He intends you harm, etc. The lam in (lakum) is either explanatory or attached to the verb, since this capacity is specific to them and for their sake. (From Allah) is a circumstantial phrase from the indefinite noun, namely "anything", placed first. Interpreting "mulk" as "prevention" is a clarification of the resulting meaning, for when no one can hold back or repel, then no one can prevent; and this is not because it is made a metaphor for it or implies it, and the lam is superfluous as in ﴿radifa lakum﴾, and (min) is connected to (yamliku), as has been said. What is meant by harm and benefit is what harms and what benefits; these are two verbal nouns, meaning what is produced by the verbal noun, or they are taken as descriptive forms.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (darran) with a damma on the dad, and it is a dialectal variant of it. The overall meaning of the verse is: say to them, since no one can repel his harm or his benefit except Him, the Exalted, so occupation with families and possessions is not an excuse; for that does not repel harm if He, mighty and majestic, intends it, nor does an enemy's surprise attack prevent benefit if He intends you benefit. This is a comprehensive reply, containing an allusion to others among the falsifiers and to the high standing of the sincere believers. Then He, glorified, progressed from this to what contains a threat, in His saying: ﴿Rather, Allah is ever, of what you do﴾, that is, of all that you do, ﴿Acquainted﴾. So He, glorified, knows your staying behind and your intention in it, and will recompense you for that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 12:

Then Exalted and Majestic God concluded with what their inner thoughts concealed and what was stored up for them with Him, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Nay, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families again﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a people doomed﴾. In al-Insaf it is said that in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So who could prevent anything from God for you﴾ and so on, there is a laff wa nashr (a rhetorical device of arranging two things and then mentioning the corresponding parts in order, without specifying the correspondence). The original is: "So who could possess anything from God for you if He intended harm for you, or who could withhold benefit from you if He intended benefit for you," because "yamliku" (to possess/control) is used in the sense of harm, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So who could possess anything from God if He intended to destroy the Messiah﴾, and ﴿And whoever God intends for him a trial, you cannot possess for him anything from God﴾, and ﴿So you cannot possess for me anything from God; He is most knowing of what you spread into it﴾. From the same usage is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, in some hadith: "(Indeed, I cannot possess anything for you)", addressing his clan, and there are many similar examples. The secret of its being specific to averting harm is that possession is construed in these places with the preposition lam, and averting harm is a benefit that is attributed to the one protected from it, whereas withholding benefit is not like that, for it is a harm that returns upon him and not to him. When this is clear, the verse is arranged in this manner because both parts share that each of them is a negation of averting what is decreed, of good and evil; and since they are close, they were included in a single expression. The expression of averting harm was singled out because it is what is expected for these people, since the verse is in the context of severe threat and warning, and it is the counterpart of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Who is it that can protect you from God if He intends harm for you, or intends mercy for you?﴾ For protection is only from evil, not from mercy. These two verses are twins in the aforementioned explanation, end of quote. The correct view is what we mentioned first regarding the verse, and calling such a thing laff wa nashr is open to question. Then, the apparent meaning is the generality of harm and benefit. Shaykh al-Islam Abu al-Su'ud said: The intended harm is what harms through the loss of family and wealth or their ruin, and the intended benefit is what benefits through the preservation of wealth and family. Generalizing them is refuted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, God has been ever Acquainted with what you do﴾, for it is a turning away from what they said and a clarification of its falsity after clarifying its corruption on the assumption of its truth, end of quote. This is a statement weaker than a spider's house, because generalization conveys what was mentioned along with an addition that gives strength and eloquence. The apparent view is that each of the three turnings (idrabat) is intended. Shaykh al-Islam said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, you thought﴾ and so on is a substitute (badal) for ﴿God has been﴾ and so on, explaining what is ambiguous in it. In al-Bahr it is said that it is an explanation of the cause of their staying behind, i.e., ﴿Nay, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return﴾ meaning would not come back from that journey ﴿to their families﴾ meaning their clans and close relatives ﴿ever﴾, by the idolaters utterly exterminating them. So you thought, if you were with them, that what befell them would befall you, and for that reason you stayed behind, not for the false excuses you mentioned. "Al-ahlun" is the plural of "ahl," and its plural is the sound plural contrary to analogy, because it is neither a proper name nor an attribute of rational beings. It is also pluralized as "ihalat," considering the feminine ta' in its singular implicitly, so it is pluralized like "tamrah" and "tamarat," and similarly "ard" and "aradat." It has come as "ihallah" with a ta' according to what is in al-Kashshaf, and it is also permissible to vowel its middle letter, so it is said "ihalat" with a fatha on the ha'. Likewise it is pluralized as "ahal," like "layali." Al-Zamakhshari applied to it the name of a collective noun (ism al-jam'), and it was said: This is a usage by him for the plural that came contrary to analogy; otherwise the condition of a collective noun according to the grammarians is that it be on the pattern of singular nouns, whether or not it has a singular. 'Abd Allah read (ila ahlihim) without the ya'. The verse makes clear that "lan" does not indicate perpetuity, and whoever claims that it does makes ﴿ever﴾ an emphasis. ﴿And that was made attractive﴾, i.e., ﴿that﴾ was made good, namely the thought implied by "you thought," ﴿in your hearts﴾, so you did not strive to remove it, and it became firmly established in you, and you occupied yourselves with your own affairs, not caring for the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and the believers. It was said: The reference is to the thing thought, which is that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and the believers would never return to their families, i.e., that was made good in your hearts so you loved it. The purpose of this is to rebuke them for their hatred of the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and the believers; and what precedes is more suitable to the context. It was also read "zayyana" in the active voice, attributing it to God, exalted is He, or to Satan. ﴿And you thought an evil thought﴾, which is their earlier thought, so its definiteness is for a known reference and it was repeated to intensify the reproach and to record the evil upon them; or it is general, so it includes that thought and all their other corrupt thoughts, among which is the thought that his prophethood is not true, for one who is firmly certain of its soundness would not dwell in his mind on what was mentioned of extermination. So it was mentioned for generalization after specification.

﴿And you were﴾ in God's eternal knowledge ﴿a people doomed﴾, i.e., perishing because of the corruption of your belief and the evil of your intention, deserving His wrath and punishment, exalted is His majesty. It was said: i.e., corrupt in your selves, hearts, and intentions, with no good in you. The apparent meaning, according to al-Bahr, is that "bur" is originally a verbal noun like "halak" (ruin), and for this reason the singular masculine is described by it in the verse of Ibn al-Zib'ara:

O Messenger of God, the King, indeed my tongue is a mender of what I have torn, while I am doomed (bur).

The feminine: Abu 'Ubayda reported "imra'ah bur" (a doomed woman), and also the dual and plural. It is also permissible that it is the plural of "ba'ir," like "ha'il" and "hul," "ha'idh" and "'udh," "bazil" and "buzl." On the verbal-noun reading, it is interpreted as an active participle. It is also permissible that "kana" means "became," i.e., you became through that thought a people perishing, deserving wrath and punishment. The apparent meaning is to keep it on its original usage and the past tense in view of knowledge, as we indicated. It was said: i.e., you were corrupt before the thought.

The words of the Exalted, ﴿And whoever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ and so on, form a new statement from Him, Mighty and Majestic. It is not part of the preceding speech that was taught. It confirms their ruin and explains its manner. That is: "And whoever does not affirm Allah the Exalted and His Messenger ﷺ, like these who stayed behind..." ﴿then indeed We have prepared﴾, meaning, made ready, ﴿for the disbelievers a blaze﴾, meaning a fire kindled, blazing and flaring. The apparent wording would have been "for them," but He turned away from that to what He mentioned, to announce that whoever does not combine belief in Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, upon him peace and blessings, is a disbeliever, and that he deserves the blaze because of his disbelief, due to the presence of the conditional linkage to a derived noun (ta'liq bil-mushtaq).

The indefiniteness of "saʻir" (blaze) serves to convey awe (tahwil), because it points to the fact that its reality cannot be known and its essence cannot be fully grasped. It was also said: it is because it is a specific fire, so the indefiniteness is for classification (tankir lil-tanwi'). The word "man" (whoever) may be understood as a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or as a conditional particle (shartiyyah). The returning pronoun from the predicate, or from the response of the conditional, is the explicit noun standing in place of the pronoun, which is the apparent form.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 14:

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.﴾ So He, mighty and majestic, is the one who disposes of all things as He wills. ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾ to forgive him, ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾ to punish him, without anyone having any influence on any part of His forgiveness, may He be exalted, or His punishment, may He be majestic and high, either in existence or in non-existence. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, exceeding in forgiveness toward whom He wills. He, glorified is He, does not will except for those for whom wisdom requires forgiveness, from among those who believe in Him, glorified is He, and in His Messenger (ﷺ). As for others among the disbelievers who openly oppose and the hypocrites, they are definitely excluded from that. In placing forgiveness first, and in concluding with His being Forgiving in the intensive form (ghafur), and in adding Merciful (rahim) to it, which also indicates intensity, rather than concluding with something that indicates His being a Punisher, there is an indication of the precedence of mercy.

And in the hadith: "Your Lord wrote upon Himself with His own hand, before He created the creation: My mercy precedes My wrath."

This precedence, as indicated in Anwar al-Tanzil, is essential (dhati). That is because forgiveness and mercy are according to the essence, while punishment is incidental (bi-l-'arad) and follows from decree and disobedience, which necessitate it. More than one scholar has stated that good is what is decreed essentially, and evil is incidental, since no particular evil exists except that it includes a universal good. This is explained in Sharh al-Hayakil.

Some of the eminent scholars said: what is meant by precedence in the hadith is the abundance of mercy and its comprehensiveness, and likewise what is meant by dominance (ghalaba) in some of the narrations. This is similar to saying: generosity dominated so-and-so. Whoever holds that mercy and wrath are among the attributes of actions does not find the matter of precedence problematic, and does not need to make it essential, as is not hidden.

According to Abu Hayyan, the verse offers some hope to those hypocrites, to the extent that they believe sincerely. It was also said: it is to cut off their empty hopes of the Prophet's (peace and blessings be upon him) seeking forgiveness for them. Al-Zamakhshari explained the first ﴿whom He wills﴾ as the one who repents, and the second as the one who persists. Then he said: He, glorified is He, expiates misdeeds by avoiding the major sins, and forgives the major sins through repentance. This is a Mu'tazili position that contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse.

Al-Tibi said: It is possible to say that His statement, exalted is He, ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾ and so on, is positioned as a conclusion (tadhyil) to His statement, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ the verse, on the basis that its counterpart from His statement ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and His Messenger, indeed We have prepared for the believers the gardens﴾ is understood as implied. Thus nothing that He restricted is restricted here, to indicate complete disposal, unrestricted will, perfect forgiveness, and all-encompassing mercy. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 15:

﴿Those who were left behind will say﴾, namely those Bedouins already mentioned; the definite article in al-Mukhallafun is for previous reference (al-lam li-l-'ahd). His saying, ﴿when you set out to take spoils, to take them﴾, is a temporal clause (zarf) governing what precedes it, not a conditional for what follows it. By "the spoils" (al-maghanim) is meant the spoils of Khaybar, as is the view of the majority of the exegetes (al-mufassirun). We have not come across any disagreement on this. It is supported by the argument that the particle sin (ﷺ indicates nearness, and Khaybar was the nearest of the spoils they set out for from al-Hudaybiyah, as you know. Thus intending it is almost certain.

It is related in authentic reports that God Most High promised the people of al-Hudaybiyah that He would compensate them with the spoils of Khaybar instead of the spoils of Makkah, if they returned in peace without gaining anything. God, glorified is He, specified this for them. That is: they will say, when you set out for the spoils of Khaybar to take them, in accordance with what God Most High promised you of them and singled you out with them, out of desire for the goods of this world, because they see the weakness of the enemy and are certain of victory. ﴿Let us follow you﴾ to Khaybar and witness with you the fighting against its people. ﴿They want to change the word of God﴾ by taking a share in the spoils which He, glorified is He, specified for the people of al-Hudaybiyah. The sum of it: they want the share which would not be attained for them without support for the religion and the raising of the word of God, Most High. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining their intention in that statement. It was said: it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (hal) of "those who were left behind", but this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

The report of the specification does not conflict with his, peace and blessings be upon him, giving some of the emigrants of Abyssinia who came with Ja'far, and some of the Daws and al-Ash'aris, from it; they are the People of the Ship, as in al-Bukhari. For that was a conferral of some of their rights upon the Muslims, or that some of it was conquered by treaty (sulh), and what he, peace and blessings be upon him, gave was part of what he had made peace over. All of this is mentioned in the biographies (siyar), but what the scholars of hadith have authenticated is that there was no treaty concerning it.

Al-Kirmani said: he, peace and blessings be upon him, gave only with the consent of the companions of the battle, or he gave from the fifth (khums) which was his right, peace and blessings be upon him. Al-Bukhari's inclination is toward the second. Interpreting the word of God as His promise to them of those spoils specifically is what Mujahid, Qatadah and the majority of the exegetes hold. Ibn Zayd said: the word of God is His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Say: you will never go out with me, ever﴾. Al-Jubba'i agreed with him on this, and many have criticized both of them, on the grounds that this was revealed concerning the hypocrites among those who stayed behind in the expedition of Tabuk, and that expedition was on a Thursday in Rajab of the ninth year, without dispute, as al-Qastallani said, while al-Hudaybiyah was in the sixth year, as Ibn al-Jawzi and others said. And this was revealed shortly after the return from al-Hudaybiyah, as you know. Also, in al-Bahr it is said: Muzaynah and Juhaynah, from these who stayed behind, went on expedition with him, peace and blessings be upon him, after this period, and after that he, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, preferred them over Tamim, Ghatafan and others from the Arabs. In al-Kashf: perhaps the one who said that intended that these who stayed behind, since they were hypocrites like those who stayed behind from Tabuk, the ruling of God Most High concerning them was one, [page 102] for the motivating cause is shared, namely their contentment with sitting at the first time. So the word of God was intended to mean His previous ruling, which is that a hypocrite is not to be taken along on expedition; and it was not intended that this ruling is analogous to that principle, or that the verse was revealed concerning them also. This is what can be made sound in its correction, end. What is said about al-Bahr can be answered: those who went on expedition later did not go until they were sincere, and they did not remain hypocrites. And God knows best.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿kalam Allah﴾ (the word of God), which is a collective noun of kind whose singular is kalimah. ﴿Say﴾ to despair them: ﴿you will never follow us﴾, that is, you shall not follow us, for it is a negation in the sense of a prohibition, for emphasis. The intention is the prohibition of them from following in what they wished to follow in, in their saying: ﴿Let us follow you﴾, which is setting out for Khaybar, as transmitted from Muhyi al-Sunnah, may mercy be upon him. It was said: the intention is "do not follow us while you have sick hearts." From Mujahid: the promise was, that is, the promise whose alteration is the changing of God Most High's word, which is His promise, glorified is He, to the people of al-Hudaybiyah, that they would not follow the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, except as volunteers, with no share in the booty. So it is as if it was said: you will not follow us except as volunteers. It was said: the intention is perpetuity, and the apparent context is the first. ﴿Thus has God said before﴾, that is, before you prepared to go out with us, and that was upon return from al-Hudaybiyah. ﴿Then they will say﴾ to the believers upon hearing this prohibition: ﴿Rather, you envy us﴾ for sharing with you in the spoils. This is a turning away from it being by God's ruling; that is, rather it is from your own selves, out of envy. Abu Haywah read (tahsidunana) with a kasra on the sin. ﴿Rather, they did not understand﴾, do not comprehend, ﴿except a little﴾, that is, except a little understanding, namely their understanding of worldly matters. It is a refutation of their false statement about the believers and a description of them with what is greater than envy and more grievous: extreme ignorance and bad understanding in matters of religion. In it is an indication of their rejection of God Most High's ruling and their affirming envy toward those noble leaders as a result of ignorance and little reflection.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 16 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say to the desert Arabs who were left behind﴾: He repeated their mention with this designation, as an intensification of blame and an indication of the heinousness of staying behind. ﴿You will be called to a people of great might﴾: possessors of strong valor and great fortitude in war. According to what Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani transmitted from al-Zuhri, they are Banu Hanifah, Musaylimah and his people, the people of al-Yamamah, and a group held this view. In another report from him, the addition is the apostates (ahl al-riddah). This was also related from al-Kalbi. And from Rafi' ibn Khadij: "We used to recite this verse in the past and did not know who they were, until Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) called for fighting Banu Hanifah, and then we knew that they were what was intended by it." And from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and Mujahid (in one report), and 'Ata' al-Khurasani and Ibn Abi Layla: they are the Persians. This was narrated by Ibn Jarir, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and others, from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj that he said concerning the verse: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) called for fighting the Persians, the desert Arabs of Madinah, Juhaynah and Muzaynah, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) had called to go out to Makkah. 'Ikrimah, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: they are Hawazin and those who fought the Messenger (ﷺ) at Hunayn. In a report of Ibn Jarir and 'Abd ibn Humayd from Qatadah, Thaqif is explicitly mentioned along with Hawazin. In a report of al-Firyabi and Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: they are Hawazin and Banu Hanifah. Ka'b said: they are the Romans, to whom the Prophet (ﷺ) went out in the year of Tabuk, and those to whom he sent (forces) in the battle of Mu'tah. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Hasan that he said: they are Persia and the Romans. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "al-Bariz," meaning the Kurds, as in al-Durr al-Manthur. Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir narrated from Mujahid that he said: "The desert Arabs of Persia and the Kurds of the non-Arabs (al-'Ajam)." The apparent sense of the conjunction is that the Kurds of the 'Ajam are not from the desert Arabs of Persia. The apparent sense of the attribution of "Kurds" to "'Ajam" indicates that among the Kurds there are those who are called "Kurds of the Arabs," but we do not recognize this division; we only know a people among mankind called:
