Akrad, without attribution to Arabs or non-Arabs. Scholars differ over whether they are originally Arabs or not: it was said they are not of the Arabs, and it was said they are of them. Qadi Shams al-Din Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khallikan, in the biography of al-Muhallab ibn Abi Sufrah, wrote the following text: Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr, author of the book al-Istay'ab, related in his book (al-Qasd wa'l-Umam fi Ansab al-'Arab wa'l-'Ajam) that the Kurds are from the descendants of 'Amr Muzayqiya ibn 'Amir ibn Ma' al-Sama', and that they came to the land of the 'Ajam, multiplied there through procreation, and their offspring increased, so they were named the Kurds. Some poets said concerning this, supporting what Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said:
By your life, the Kurds are not sons of Persia, but rather Kurd ibn 'Amr ibn 'Amir.
End of quote. In the Qamus: "al-Kurd, with a damma, is a known people of mankind, and the plural is Akrad, and their grandfather is Kurd ibn 'Amr Muzayqiya ibn 'Amir Ma' al-Sama'." End of quote. This 'Amir is without doubt from the Arabs, for he is the son of Haritha al-Ghitrif ibn Imru' al-Qays al-Bitriq ibn Tha'labah ibn Mazin ibn al-Azd, and he is also called al-Asad ibn al-Ghawth ibn Nabt ibn Malik ibn Zayd ibn Kahlan ibn Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan, and he is called 'Amir. According to most, he is the son of Shalakh ibn Arfakhshadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh. It was said he is from the offspring of Hud, and it was said he is Hud himself, and it was said he is the brother of Hud's son. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar held that Qahtan is from the descendants of Isma'il (peace be upon him), and that he is Qahtan ibn al-Hamaysa' ibn Tim ibn Nabt ibn Isma'il. What Ibn Hajar preferred is that all the tribes of Yemen, including the tribe of 'Amr Muzayqiya, are from the offspring of Isma'il (peace be upon him). This is supported by al-Bukhari's chapter heading: "The attribution of Yemen to Isma'il (peace be upon him)," as mentioned by al-Sayyid Nur al-Din 'Ali al-Samhudi in Tarikh al-Madinah. In it, the Ansar, al-Aws and al-Khazraj, are from the sons of Tha'labah al-'Anqa' ibn 'Amr Muzayqiya mentioned above, who had thirteen male sons, including the aforementioned Tha'labah, Haritha, father of Khuza'ah, Jafnah, father of Ghassan, Wada'ah, Abu Haritha, 'Awf, Ka'b, Malik, 'Imran, and Kurd, as in the Qamus. End of quote.

The benefit of the disagreement appears in matters including suitability (kafa'ah) in marriage. The common people do not count them among the Arabs, so take note. What most strongly prevails in my opinion is that this generation who today are called Kurds may well include some who are from the sons of 'Amr Muzayqiya, and likewise it is not far-fetched that among them are some who are from the Arabs, though not from the sons of the aforementioned 'Amr. Yet most of them are not of Arab origin at all. Into this category have been grouped people who are said to be descendants of Khalid ibn al-Walid, others said to be descendants of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and others said to be descendants of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and others said to be from Banu Umayyah. None of this is authentic in my view, except that a group of noble descendants of al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with them) lived among the Kurds, called the Barazanjiyyah. There is no doubt about the soundness of their lineage, nor about the nobility of their stock. In sum, the Kurds are well known for valor, and many people of virtue have come from them; indeed, companionship (suhbah) was established for some of them. The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Isabah fi Tamyiz al-Sahabah, under the letter Jim: Jaban, father of Maymun, was narrated by Ibn Mandah through the route of Abu Sa'id, client of Banu Hashim, from Abu Khaladah: I heard Maymun ibn Jaban al-Kurdi from his father that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) more than once, until he reached ten, and he mentioned the hadith.

Al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Saghir narrated something similar from Maymun al-Kurdi from his father as well, and it is more complete. Its wording: (I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whichever man marries a woman for a dowry, whether small or large, while in his heart he does not intend to pay her what is due to her, has deceived her; if he dies without paying her what is due, he will meet Allah on the Day of Resurrection as an adulterer. And whichever man borrows a debt, not intending to pay its creditor his due, has deceived him until he takes his wealth; if he dies without paying the debt, he will meet Allah as a thief.")

This Maymun is known by the kunyah Abu Basir, with the letter ba' pointed, and it was said with the letter nun; he is, as in al-Taqrib, acceptable (maqbul). That said, the most famous opinion in identifying these people is that they are Banu Hanifah.

Abu Hayyan said: "What I say is that these statements are examples given by their speakers, not specifications of the people." Although the combining of those statements is achieved by this, it is contrary to the apparent sense. The words of Allah Most High ﴿you will fight them or they will submit﴾ mean that one of the two matters must occur, either fighting or Islam, with no third. Here "aw" is for enumeration and restriction, not for doubt, and this usage is common. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy and Zayd ibn 'Ali, "aw yuslimu" (without the nun), because that is the form after a subjunctive particle, which requires that "aw" carries the meaning of "illa" (except), i.e., "except that they submit," which gives restriction; or the meaning of "ila" (until), i.e., "until they submit," and the limit implies that fighting does not end except by Islam, which also conveys this. As it has been said, the clause is a new sentence giving the reason, as in your saying: "The commander will call you; he will honor you or he will humble your enemy." In al-Kashf it is said: it cannot be a description of "a people," because they were called to fight a people, not called to a people described as fighting or submitting.

Some have permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal), and its status is like that of the descriptive clause. The original wording would be: "You will be called to a people of great might, so that you fight them or they submit," but it shifted to a new sentence, because that is the more eloquent of the two connections. Then in it is the sense that they did this and achieved the aim, so it reports on it as an actual event.

The objection that it would follow that existence cannot be free of one of the two, since His report is true while we see separation, by their being left unfought or by a truce, so it should be interpreted as having the sense of a command, as in Ibn al-Hajib's Amali, is not sound, because the people are specific, with no generality among them. What actually happened is that they were fought until they submitted, whether the people are explained as Banu Hanifah, or Thaqif and Hawazin, or Persia and the Romans, on the basis that Islam means submission. Thus existence was not separated from one of the two. As for the impossibility of separation, it is not required by the lexical form nor by usage; rather, it may happen in argumentative discourse.

Al-Tibi extended the discussion on this point, then said: "What the context requires is what the author of al-Tahbir went to, that ﴿they submit﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you fight them﴾, either on its apparent form or by taking it as ﴿they submit﴾ so that it is a nominal clause coordinated with a verbal clause. Then the fit is greater, as the sentence enters the domain of metonymy (kinayah). The meaning is: you fight them or you do not fight them, because they submit; and ﴿or they submit﴾ has been placed in the position of 'or you do not fight them,' because when they submit, fighting them falls away necessarily. The calling to it is only for testing, and 'or' is for alternation by way of metaphor, and there is in this what there is." It is widely known that the verse is used as evidence for the validity of the imamate of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him). The Imam (al-Razi) argued this way: the caller in His words ﴿you will be called﴾ must be either the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or the four Imams, or those after them. The first is impossible, because of His words ﴿Say: You will by no means follow us﴾ etc. Nor can it be 'Ali (may Allah honor his face), because he fought the rebels and the Kharijites, and that fighting was for Islam, given His words ﴿or they submit﴾. Nor can it be any ruler after them, because according to us they were in error, and according to the Shi'ah they were in disbelief. Since all the divisions are invalid, it is necessarily determined that the intended caller is Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with them). Further, He made obedience to him obligatory and threatened those who oppose him, and that requires his imamate; whichever of the three it was, the claim is established. If it is Abu Bakr, it is obvious; if it is 'Umar or 'Uthman, it is because their imamate is derived from his imamate (may Allah be pleased with him). It was objected that the caller was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the letter sin in "sa-" indicates this, and that the statement "it is not permissible" rests on His words "You will by no means follow us," etc. It is said that "lan" does not confer perpetuity according to the correct view, and the apparent context indicates that what is meant is "You will by no means follow us in setting out for Khaybar," as you have heard from Muhyi al-Sunnah, or it is restricted to what was related from Mujahid, or to what was reported from some. Abu Hayyan said: the claim that they were not called to war in the days of the Messenger (ﷺ) is not correct, for many of them attended Mu'tah with Ja'far, and they attended the battle of Hawazin with him (peace be upon him), and they attended with him (ﷺ) also in the expedition of Tabuk. End of quote. It is not hidden that this, if sound, negates taking the negation as perpetual.

Among the Shi'a are those who limited their rebuttal of the argument to the summons at Tabuk. It was objected to that what Allah the Exalted announced in His saying, ﴿You will fight them, or they will submit﴾, did not occur in it. Among them is one who claimed that the one summoning was Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and claimed the disbelief of the rebels (al-bughat) and the Kharijites against him, may Allah be pleased with him, and that even if their submission were granted, "submission" in the verse would mean submission to obedience and loyalty to the commander. There is in this what is not hidden. The fair judgment is that the verse hardly serves as a valid proof for the imamate of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, unless a reliable hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) establishes that the intended people are the Banu Hanifa and their like; anything short of that is like trying to pluck thorns with bare hands (kharth al-qatad).

Some of them denied the correctness of taking the people to be Persia and the Romans, because the intended meaning in His saying, ﴿You will fight them, or they will submit﴾, as you have heard, is that Persia are Magians and the Romans are Christians, so neither of the two alternatives of fighting and submission is specifically fixed for them, since the jizya (poll tax) is accepted from them. The same applies to the Jews, the non-Arab polytheists, and the Sabians, according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him. He said: it is specifically necessary that they be apostates or Arab polytheists, because they are the ones from whom nothing is accepted except Islam or the sword. Similar to the Arab polytheists are the non-Arab polytheists according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him; for him, nothing is accepted except from the People of the Book and the Magians.

You know that whoever interprets "the people" in this way interprets "submission" as "submission to authority," and that is achieved by accepting the jizya; so the matter of negation is not complete for him. So do not overlook this.

﴿But if you obey﴾ the summoner in what he calls you to, ﴿Allah will give you a good reward﴾, which, as it has been said, is booty in this world and Paradise in the Hereafter. ﴿But if you turn away﴾ from the summons, ﴿as you turned away before﴾ at al-Hudaybiyya, ﴿He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾ because of the multiplication of your sin. Regarding this punishment, al-Bahr says: it may be in this world and it may be in the Hereafter. In my view, and it is more fitting with what precedes it, as has been said, it is possible that it is in both; and there is no harm in both the giving and the punishment being in the Hereafter. Indeed, this is perhaps the most immediately understood meaning, due to the frequency of using these two terms in that sense. It is not fitting that both matters be in this world, nor that the first be in the Hereafter, or in both, while the second is in this world alone.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 17:

﴿There is no blame upon the blind man﴾, i.e., no sin, ﴿nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, any blame﴾, i.e., in staying behind from the military expedition (ghazw), because of the excuse and infirmity they have. The negation of blame from each of the groups enumerated indicates extra care for their situation and an extension of the scope of the dispensation (rukhsah). The negation of blame from them does not constitute a prohibition for them from the expedition; rather, they said: "Their reward is doubled in the expedition." Ibn Umm Maktum, who was blind, radiyallahu ta'ala anhu, took part in the expedition and was present at some of the battles of al-Qadisiyyah, and he was holding the banner. In al-Bahr: if the Muslims are besieged, the obligation of jihad falls upon each according to his capacity. ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾, in what has been mentioned of commands and prohibitions.

﴿He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, and whoever turns away﴾ from obedience ﴿He will punish him with a painful punishment﴾ whose extent cannot be measured. The meaning of promise and threat here is more general than their meaning in what preceded, as indicated by the expression "whoever" (man) here and the second-person pronoun there. It has been said that in the threat, the wording ﴿He will punish him﴾ etc. is used instead of "He will admit him to the Fire" or the like, which is more evidently in contrast with His saying, ﴿He will admit him to gardens﴾ etc., out of concern for his matter, since punishment on the Day of Resurrection with a painful punishment entails admission to the Fire, whereas admission to it does not necessarily entail that. He gave it this concern because the context requires it, and therefore it came almost as a repetition alongside the earlier threat. Mentioning the promise here, as an elaboration of what came before, suffices to indicate that mercy has preceded; and the expression there, "giving a good reward," which apparently signifies entitlement, together with attributing the giving to the Glorious Name Himself, is noteworthy, so reflect. The path of the mind is broad.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Shaybah, Ibn 'Amir and Nafi' read (nudkhilhu) and (nu'adhdhibhu) with the letter nun in both.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 18 (part 1 of 2):

When the Exalted (subhanahu) mentioned the condition of those who stayed behind from journeying with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), He, may He be Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the condition of the sincere believers who journeyed with him (peace be upon him) by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾. They were the People of al-Hudaybiyya, except Jadd ibn Qays, for he was a hypocrite and did not pledge allegiance.

The origin of this pledge, which is called the Pledge of Good Pleasure (Bay'at al-Ridwan), is due to the saying of Allah, may He be exalted, concerning it: ﴿Allah was certainly pleased﴾ etc., that: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) alighted at al-Hudaybiyya, he sent Khirash, with a kasra on the kha' (kh), a fath on the ra' (r) (unpointed), and an alif after it, followed by a shin (sh) with a dot, Ibn Umayya al-Khuza'i, as a messenger to the people of Makkah, and he carried him on a camel of his called al-Tha'lab, informing them that he had come performing 'umrah, not desiring fighting. When he came to them and spoke with them, they hamstrung his camel and intended to kill him, but the Ahabish prevented them, and they released his way until he came to the Messenger (ﷺ). So he (ﷺ) called Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) to send him, but he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the people know of my enmity toward them and my harshness against them, and I am not safe. There is no one in Makkah from the Banu 'Adi who would be angered for me if I were harmed. So send Uthman ibn Affan, for his clan is there, and they love him, and he will convey what you desire.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Uthman and sent him to the Quraysh, and said: 'Inform them that we have not come for fighting, but we have come as pilgrims (for 'umrah), and invite them to Islam.'

He (peace be upon him) commanded him to go to men in Makkah who were believers, and to women who were believers, and to give them the good news of the conquest, and to inform them that Allah, may He be exalted, will soon make His religion prevail in Makkah. Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) went to the Quraysh. Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As had met him, so he dismounted from his mount, carried him upon it, and gave him protection. He then came to the Quraysh and informed them. They said to him: 'If you wish, circumambulate the House (the Ka'bah). As for your entering upon us, there is no way to that.' He (may Allah be pleased with him) said: 'I would not circumambulate it until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) circumambulates it.' So they detained him. The news reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims that Uthman had been killed. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'We will not depart until we engage the people.' And his caller called out (peace be upon him): 'Indeed Ruh al-Qudus (the Holy Spirit) has descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he commanded him to the pledge. So set out in the name of Allah, may He be exalted.' So they pledged allegiance to him, and the Muslims rushed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and pledged allegiance to him."

Jabir said, as in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere: "We pledged allegiance to him (ﷺ) that we would not flee, and we did not pledge allegiance to him for death."

Al-Bukhari narrated from Salamah ibn al-Akwa' who said: "I pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) under the tree." It was said: "On what did you pledge allegiance that day?" He said: "On death."

Muslim narrated from Ma'qil ibn Yasar that he was holding the branches of the tree away from the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was taking the pledge from the people. The first person who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that day was Abu Sinan, who was Wahb ibn Mihsan, the brother of 'Ukkashah ibn Mihsan. It was also said: Sinan ibn Abi Sinan. Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated the first (version) from al-Sha'bi, and that he "said to the Prophet (peace be upon him): 'Extend your hand, and I will pledge allegiance to you.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'For what do you pledge allegiance to me?' He said: 'For what is in your heart.'" In the hadith of Jabir narrated by Muslim, he said: "We pledged allegiance to him (peace be upon him) while Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) was holding his hand." Perhaps that was not at the beginning of the pledge. Otherwise, in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Nafi', that Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) on the day of al-Hudaybiyya sent his son Abdullah to a man of the Ansar, to bring his horse for him to fight upon it, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taking the pledge at the tree, and Umar did not know of that. Abdullah pledged allegiance, then went to the horse and brought it to Umar, while Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) was putting on his armour for battle. He informed him that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taking the pledge under the tree. So he set off and went with him until he pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

It is authentically related that "he (ﷺ) struck his right hand upon his left and said: 'This is the pledge of Uthman.'" When the polytheists heard of the pledge, they feared, and they sent Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) and a group of Muslims. The number of believers was one thousand four hundred, according to the more accurate view of most of the scholars of hadith. Al-Bukhari narrated it from Jabir. It is also related from Sa'id ibn Qatadah who said: "I said to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: 'It has reached me that Jabir ibn Abdullah used to say: They were fourteen hundred.' Sa'id said to me: 'Jabir narrated to me that they were fifteen hundred who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'" Abu Dawud also narrated similarly. It is also related from Abdullah ibn Awfa who said: "The companions of the tree were one thousand three hundred." In the work of Abu Shaybah, from the hadith of Salamah ibn al-Akwa', they were one thousand seven hundred. Musa ibn Uqbah affirmed that they were one thousand six hundred. Ibn Sa'd related that they were one thousand five hundred and twenty-five. The reports were reconciled by saying that they are based on counting everyone, or leaving out the young and the followers and the middling ones, or something similar. As for the statement of Ibn Ishaq that they were seven hundred, no one agreed with him, because he said it by deduction from the saying of Jabir: "A camel is slaughtered on behalf of ten," and they had slaughtered seventy camels. This does not indicate that they slaughtered nothing other than camels, especially since some of them, like Abu Qatadah, had not entered the state of ihram at all. The tree was a samurah (acacia-type tree). It is well known that people used to come to it and pray beside it. Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) learned of this and ordered it cut down, for fear of temptation through it, given their closeness to the Jahiliyyah and the worship of other than Allah among them.

In the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of Tariq ibn Abd al-Rahman, who said: "I set out as a pilgrim and passed by a people praying. I said: 'What is this place of worship?' They said: 'This is the tree where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the Pledge of Good Pleasure.' So I came to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and informed him. He said: 'My father told me that he was among those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) under the tree.' He said: 'When the following year came, we forgot it and could not find it.' Then Sa'id said: 'The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not know it, but you know it. So which of you is more knowledgeable?'"

Al-Rida (good pleasure) is the opposite of al-sakhat (displeasure). It may be used with 'an and with the bi' (preposition ba'), and it may be transitive by itself. With 'an, it only enters upon the (physical) entity, not the meaning, but it does so by considering that a meaning proceeds from it which necessitates pleasure, and this is the case in the verse. The meaning that necessitates pleasure in it is the pledge. When a meaning is mentioned with the entity using bi', as when one says "I am pleased with Zayd for his kindness," the ba' is for causation (sababiyyah). It may also be a particle (silah), and it is specifically causal when contrasted with a construction like "I was angry with him for his wrongdoing." With bi', as in "I am pleased with him," it must enter upon the meaning, except when it enters upon the essence as a preparation for the meaning, to make it more emphatic, as when you say: "I am pleased with the decree of Allah, the Exalted," and "I am pleased with Allah, the Exalted, as Lord and Judge." When it is transitive by itself, it may enter upon the essence, as in "I am pleased with Zayd," even though according to the meaning, it is an indication that all of him is pleasing in that quality, and this carries emphasis. It may also enter upon the meaning, as in "I am pleased with the amirate of so-and-so." The first is more common in usage. When it is used with the lam (li), it is transitive by itself, as in your saying: "I am pleased for you with trade." There is a figurative extension in this, either by making the good pleasure a metaphor for praise, or because you have made his being pleasing to him equivalent to his being pleasing to you, as an emphasis that he is in himself pleasing and praiseworthy, and that you choose for him what you choose for yourself. This is more eloquent.

Then, with regard to the Real, the Exalted in His majesty, it is considered impossible according to the dissenters, who say: "Because He, glorified be He, has no quality that comes into being after any event whatsoever." So for them it is a metaphor, either from the names of attributes, if it is interpreted as intending that He rewards them as one who is pleased rewards those under his authority, or from the names of actions, if it is interpreted as reward. Likewise, if the intent is praise. In al-Bahr it is said that the governing element of idh (إذْ) in the verse is radiya (رَضِيَ), and here it means the manifestation of blessings upon them. So it is a description of action, not a description of essence, to be restricted by time. You know that the salaf (early generations) do not interpret such things figuratively, but affirm them for Him in the manner befitting Him, glorified be He, and they explain the occurrence that the restriction by time requires as relating to the connection (ta'alluq). Furthermore, restricting the good pleasure to the time of the pledge indicates that the pledge is its cause, so there is no need to make idh (إذْ) indicate causation. The use of the present tense (yubayi'unaka) is to bring the image of the pledge before the mind. The Exalted's saying ﴿under the tree﴾ is either connected to yubayi'unaka, or to something elided which is a circumstantial clause (hal) of its object. Mentioning it with this specification indicates the great impact of that pledge, and that it was not out of fear from him (peace be upon him). For this reason it merited the good pleasure of Allah, than which nothing is equal, and it entails what hardly occurs to the mind. What suffices concerning what resulted from that is what Ahmad narrated from Jabir, and Muslim from Umm Bashar, from him (Jabir), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "None of those who pledged allegiance under the tree will enter the Fire."

He (peace be upon him) said that to Hafsah, and she said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah," so he rebuked her. She then said: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾. He (peace be upon him) said: "Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Then We will save those who feared Allah, and leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees﴾."

It is authentically related, through the narration of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others, concerning those believers, from the hadith of Jabir, that he (peace be upon him) said to them: "You are the best of the people of the earth."

Therefore, it is incumbent upon everyone who claims Islam to love them, honour them, and be pleased with them. And whatever else (than that) does not harm them after the good pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, toward them. Uthman is one of them. Indeed, the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was for him (may Allah be pleased with him) better, as Anas said, than their hands for themselves. ﴿So He knew what was in their hearts﴾, that is, of truthfulness and sincerity in their pledge. Similar is related from Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Farra'. Al-Tabari and Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: "(It is) of faith, its soundness, love of the religion, and eagerness for it." It was also said: "(It is) of concern and resentment at being gentle toward the polytheists and making peace with them." Abu Hayyan approved this, but the first (view) is, in my opinion, the best.

This (clause) is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon (yubayi'unaka), because of what you know, that it has the meaning of "they pledged to you." It is permissible for it to be coordinated upon (radiya) by interpreting it as "the manifestation of His knowledge," so that it becomes a consequence of the good pleasure, being ordered upon it. ﴿Then He sent down tranquillity upon them﴾, that is, serenity, security, calm of the soul, and steadying of their hearts through encouragement. It was also said: "through making peace," but that is not the case. The apparent (meaning) is that it is coordinated upon (fa-alima, فَعَلِمَ).

[p. 107]

In the Irshad (of Abu al-Su'ud), it is stated that it is coordinated with (radiya, "was pleased"). The apparent sense of Abu Hayyan's words is the first view. Since he approved of explaining what is in the hearts by what you have just heard, he said: "Here, sakina (tranquillity) means the steadying of their hearts and their being made submissive to accept the command of Allah the Exalted." Muqatil said: "Allah knew what was in their hearts of aversion to pledging to fight alongside Him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, unto death. So He sent down sakina upon them until they pledged allegiance." Sakina is also explained as the making submissive of their hearts and the removal of their aversion to the pledge. By my life, this man did not recognize the rights of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and he took the words of Allah the Exalted contrary to their apparent meaning.

﴿And He rewarded them with a near victory﴾. Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Qatadah, Ibn Abi Layla and others said: it is the conquest of Khaybar, which took place shortly after they returned from al-Hudaybiyah. Al-Hasan said: it is the conquest of Hajar, and the intended meaning is Hajar of Bahrain, which was conquered during his lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as evidenced by his letter to Amr ibn Hazm concerning the zakat and blood-money.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, it is reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made a treaty with the people of Bahrain and took the jizya from the Magians of Hajar. A conquest does not require a prior military expedition, as you know from what preceded in its explanation. Thus the statement of al-Tibi, objecting to al-Hasan, that none of the imams mentioned that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, campaigned against Hajar, falls away. Indeed, applying the term "conquest" to such a case is rare and not common; rather, it is said to be a figurative meaning of it. It is also said that it is the conquest of Mecca, and "near" is a relative matter.

And al-Hasan and Nuh al-Qari read (wa-atahum), meaning: He gave them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 19:

﴿And much booty that they will take﴾. It is the booty of Khaybar, as said by more than one (scholar), and the Prophet (ﷺ) divided it as is mentioned in the hadith of Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, from Mujammi' ibn Jariya al-Ansari: he gave the horseman two shares, and there were three hundred horsemen among them, and to the foot soldier one share. And it is said: (the booty) of Hajar. Al-A'mash, Talha, and Ruways from Ya'qub, and Dulbah from Yunus from Warsh, and Abu Dihya and Siqlab from Nafi', and al-Antaki from Abu Ja'far read (taʾkhudunaha) with the taʾ on top (i.e., in the second person), and the shift to the address (second person) is for their honour in the context of the favour (bestowed upon them). ﴿And Allah has ever been Almighty﴾, dominant, ﴿Wise﴾, observant of what wisdom requires in His rulings and decrees, exalted is His majesty.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 20:

﴿Allah has promised you abundant spoils that you will take﴾. According to what Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and the majority of the exegetes said, this refers to the spoils that Allah the Exalted promised the believers until the Day of Resurrection, ﴿that you will take﴾ at their appointed times, each of which is determined. ﴿So He hastened this for you﴾, that is, the spoils of Khaybar, ﴿and restrained the hands of the people from you﴾, that is, the hands of the people of Khaybar and their allies from the Banu Asad and Ghatafan, when they came to support them. Allah the Exalted cast terror into their hearts, so they turned back. Mujahid said: He restrained the hands of the people of Makkah through the peace treaty. al-Tabari said: He restrained the Jews from Madinah after the Messenger (ﷺ) departed to al-Hudaybiyah and to Khaybar. Zayd ibn Aslam and his son said: The abundant spoils that were promised are the spoils of Khaybar, and the one hastened is the pledge (of allegiance) and the deliverance from the affair of the Quraysh through the peace treaty. The majority hold to what we have already presented. The connection to what preceded, the mention of the Prophet (ﷺ) by way of address and elsewhere by way of the third person, as in His saying: ﴿Certainly Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you﴾, requires, according to what has been reported from some of the eminent scholars, that this follows the method of gently preferring one party (taghlib), although it may admit of a shift in address here. Al-Jalabi, in regard to His saying ﴿So He hastened this for you﴾ etc., mentioned that if its revelation was after the conquest of Khaybar, as is apparent, then the surah in its entirety was not revealed on the return of the Messenger (ﷺ) from al-Hudaybiyah; and if it was before that, on the basis that it is information about the unseen, then the reference by "this" is to make the spoils present and witnessed, and the expression in the past tense is for certainty. The end of his words. The first alternative was chosen. As for the statement of those who say it was revealed on the return of the Messenger (ﷺ) from al-Hudaybiyah, this is considered in terms of the majority, or it is taken in its apparent sense, but the return is made a name of an extended period of time. It has been criticized that the apparent meaning of the reports requires that there be no extension, and that it was revealed from its beginning to its end between Makkah and Madinah; so perhaps the preferable option is the second alternative. The reference by "this" is to the spoils that He bestowed upon them, mentioned in His saying: ﴿And He rewarded them with a near victory﴾ and ﴿abundant spoils that you will take﴾, and these are the spoils of Khaybar. When the reference is made to the pledge (of allegiance), as was heard from Zayd and his son, and it is narrated the same from Ibn ʿAbbas, there is no need for an interpretation of its revelation on the return of the Messenger (ﷺ) from al-Hudaybiyah. ﴿And that it may be a sign for the believers﴾. The hidden pronoun: it has been said that it refers to the restraint understood from ﴿restrained﴾, and the feminine form is according to the predicate; and it has been said that it refers to the "kaffah" (the act of restraining), so the feminine form is apparent.

It is also permitted that it refers to the spoils of Khaybar indicated by "this," and that "the sign" means the token, i.e., that it may be a token for the believers by which they know that they are in a position with Allah the Exalted, or by which they know the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) in his promise to them of the conquest of Khaybar, the spoils mentioned, the conquest of Makkah, and entering the Sacred Mosque. The lam is connected either to an omitted, postponed element, meaning: and that it may be a sign for them of what He did, or to another omitted cause from one of the two preceding verbs, meaning: He hastened this for you, or restrained the hands of the people from you, so that you may benefit by that and that it may be a sign. Thus the waw, as in al-Irshad, according to the first, is parenthetical, and according to the second, it is conjunctive. According to the Kufans, the waw is extra, and the lam is connected to "restrained" or to "hastened." ﴿And guide you﴾ by that sign ﴿to a straight path﴾, which is trust in the grace of Allah the Exalted and reliance upon Him in everything you do and leave undone.

[Page 110]

﴿And another﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with ﴿this﴾ in ﴿He has hastened this for you﴾. The sense is as if it were said: "He has hastened for you these spoils, and He has hastened for you other spoils," and these are the spoils of Hawazin in the battle of Hunayn. "Hastening" is relative to what comes after, so it is permissible for the thing hastened to be more than one, as in beginning with two things. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿you were not able to gain them﴾, is in the place of a qualifier (ṣifah). He described them as beyond their power because of the turmoil they had experienced in them before that, in order to increase their desire for them. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Allah has already encompassed them﴾, is in the place of another qualifier for "another," conveying the ease of obtaining them relative to His power, mighty and majestic is He, after explaining the difficulty of attaining them relative to their own power. "Encompassing" is a metaphor (majāz) for complete control, meaning: Allah has indeed had power over them and has taken control of them, so they are within the grip of His power, exalted is He; He causes whomever He wills to prevail over them. Indeed, He, whose majesty is great, has made you prevail over them and granted you victory over them. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for protection, meaning: He has indeed guarded them for you and prevented them from others. The concluding statement, glorified is He, ﴿and Allah is ever, over all things, Competent﴾, is more suitable to the first meaning. The generality of His power, exalted is He, is because it is required by His essence, so it cannot change, nor can it be contrary to it, nor can it be removed from the essence by any cause, as has been established in its proper place. Thus its relation to all things that are within power is equal, without being specific to some over others; otherwise it would be varied, indeed differing.

It has also been permitted that ﴿another﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a verb that the phrase ﴿Allah has already encompassed them﴾ explains, like "qad qaḍā" (He has decreed).

It was objected that the report of Allah's decree, exalted is He, after it was included in the category of spoils promised in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Allah has promised you many spoils that you will take﴾, has no added benefit; the benefit lies only in clarifying its hastening. It was answered that the many promised spoils are not specified, so that the other could be included among them. And even if this were granted, the intended benefit is not that it is decreed, but what follows it, so reflect.

It has also been permitted that it is in the nominative, by way of the inchoative (mubtada'), with the sentence after it being a qualifier and the sentence ﴿has already encompassed them﴾ its predicate (khabar). Abu Hayyan preferred this view. Some said that the predicate is omitted, its estimate being "there is," or something similar. al-Zamakhshari permitted that it is in the genitive by implying "rubba" (many a), as in the line:

"And a night like the waves of the sea has let down its curtains."

Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that it is strange, because rubba has not come in the Mighty Qur'an as a governing particle, despite its frequent occurrence in Arabic speech, so how could it be implied here? You know that such strangeness does no harm.

This interpretation of "another" as the spoils of Hawazin was narrated by Abd ibn Humayd from Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, and many have chosen it. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: it is Makkah, and they had attempted it in the year of Hudaybiyyah but did not reach it, so they were informed that Allah, exalted is He, would grant them victory over it and make them prevail over it. In another narration from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan, and it is narrated from Muqatil, it is the lands of Persia and Byzantium and what the Muslims would conquer. This is not apparent according to the interpretation of the many spoils promised earlier as what Allah promised the Muslims of spoils until the Day of Resurrection. Also, some have objected to it, saying that ﴿you were not able to gain them﴾ implies a previous attempt at those lands and the failure to attain what was sought, whereas no previous attempt had been made.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: it is Khaybar. This was also narrated from al-Dahhak, Ishaq, and Ibn Zayd. There is some obscurity in it, so do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 22:

﴿And if those who disbelieve had fought you﴾ — i.e., from the people of Makkah — and had not made peace with you, as has been narrated from Qatadah. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj that they were allies of the people of Khaybar: Asad and Ghatafan. It is also said that they were the Jews, but this is not correct. ﴿they would have turned their backs⦆ — i.e., they would have been routed. Thus "turning the back" (tawliyat al-dubur) is a metaphor (kinayah) for defeat. ﴿Then they would not find a protector⦆ — one who would guard them. Al-Khafaji mentioned that "guardian" (al-haris) is one of the meanings of al-wali (protector), and interpreting it here in that sense suits the context of the one who is routed. Al-Raghib said: whoever takes charge of another's affairs is his wali, and accordingly the guardian is a wali because he takes charge of the affairs of the one he guards. The indefinite form is for generalisation, i.e., they would not find any single protector from among the protectors ﴿nor a helper⦆ — nor any single one of the helpers who would support them. Al-Imam said: by al-wali is meant the one who benefits by gentleness (al-lutf), and by al-nasir the one who benefits by force (al-unf).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 23:

﴿Sunnat Allah (the way of God) which has already passed before, [and] you will never find any change in the way of God.﴾ Here "sunnat" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), governed by a verb omitted from the sentence, meaning: He, glorified is He, has established the victory of His prophets, peace be upon them, as an ancient practice (sunnah) regarding those nations who passed away, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿I and My messengers will surely prevail﴾, according to what is most apparent from its meaning. Perhaps the intended meaning is that it is God's practice (sunnah) that the final outcome belongs to His prophets, peace be upon them, not that whenever they fought the disbelievers they defeated and routed them. ﴿And you will never find any change in the way of God﴾, meaning, any alteration.

He it is who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the heart of Makkah, after He had given you victory over them. The restraining of their hands refers to the hands of the disbelievers of Makkah. The use of the verb "restrained" (kaffa) rather than "prevented" (mana'a) or similar is a subtle delicacy that is not hidden. "In the heart of Makkah" means al-Hudaybiyah, as 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah. It has already been mentioned that part of it lies within the sacred precinct (haram) of Makkah. If it is not within the sacred precinct, then close proximity is sufficient, and calling it "the heart of Makkah" is a form of hyperbole. "After He had given you victory over them" means making you prevail over them. The verb takes "over" ('ala) because it includes the meaning of what is transitive with it, namely making prevail and exalting, that is, He made you possessors of complete dominance.

Imam Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others reported from Anas, who said: "When it was the day of al-Hudaybiyah, eighty men from the people of Makkah descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions, armed, from the direction of the mountain of al-Tan'im, intending to catch the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) off guard. He invoked (Allah) against them and they were seized, but he pardoned them. Then this verse was revealed: 'He it is who restrained their hands...' etc."

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il reported "from 'Abd Allah ibn Ma'qil, who said: 'We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the base of the tree which Allah mentions in the Qur'an,' up to his saying: 'While we were like that, there came out upon us thirty young men with weapons, and they rushed at our faces. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked (Allah) against them, and Allah seized their ears' (and the wording of al-Hakim is 'their eyes'). We stood up to them and seized them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: 'Did you come under a covenant with anyone, or did anyone grant you safe conduct?' They said: 'No.' So he released them, and Allah revealed: 'He it is who restrained their hands from you...' etc."

Ahmad and others reported from Salamah ibn al-Akwa', who said: "We came to al-Hudaybiyah with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and we were fourteen hundred. Then the polytheists of Makkah sent to us seeking a truce. When we had made peace and some of us mixed with others, I came to a tree, lay down in its shade, and there came to me four of the polytheists of the people of Makkah, and they began to speak ill of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I hated them, so I moved to another tree. They hung up their weapons and lay down. While they were like that, a caller called out from below, from the direction of the Muhajirun: 'Ibn Zanim has been killed!' I drew my sword and rushed upon those four while they were asleep. I took their weapons and held them in my hand. Then I said: 'By He who honoured the face of Muhammad, none of you may raise his head except that I strike the one in whom are his two eyes.' Then I brought them, driving them before me, to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). My uncle 'Amir came with a man of the polytheists called Mukarraz, leading him, until we stood with them before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), along with seventy of the polytheists. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at them and said: 'Leave them. They will bear the beginning of the wickedness and its repetition.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pardoned them, and Allah revealed: 'He it is who restrained...' etc." All of this supports what we have said.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abza, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) set out with the sacrificial animals and reached Dhu al-Hulayfah, my uncle said to him: 'O Prophet of Allah, you are entering upon a people who are at war with you without weapons or horses.' So he sent to Madinah, and he left no horses or weapons there without bringing them. When he approached Makkah, they prevented him from entering, so he travelled until he came to Mina and alighted there. Then his spy came to him to say that 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl had gathered five hundred against you.' He said to Khalid ibn al-Walid: 'O Khalid, this is your cousin who has come to you with horses.' Khalid said: 'I am the Sword of Allah and the Sword of His Messenger.' That day he was named 'Sword of Allah.' 'O Messenger of Allah, send me if you wish.' So he dispatched him with horses. 'Ikrimah met him in the mountain pass, and he defeated him until he drove him to the walls of Makkah. Then Allah revealed: 'He it is who...' the verse."

In al-Bahr it is stated that Khalid defeated them until they entered the houses of Makkah, and he captured a group of them, who were brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he bestowed favour upon them and released them. But the report is not authentic, because Khalid's conversion (may Allah be pleased with him) came after al-Hudaybiyah and before the 'Umrat al-Qada'. It is also said that it came after it, and that was in the seventh year.

Ibn Ishaq and others reported that "on the day of al-Hudaybiyah, Khalid was over the horses of Quraysh, two hundred horsemen, whom he brought to Kura' al-Ghamim. He approached until he saw the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered 'Abbad ibn Bishr, who advanced with his horses and stood opposite him, and he arranged his companions. When the time of the Zuhr prayer came, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed with his companions the prayer of fear." And from Ibn 'Abbas, that the people of Makkah sent a number of horsemen to al-Hudaybiyah wishing to attack the Muslims, but Allah made them prevail over them with stones until they drove them into the houses. Some scholars denied this report, and Allah knows best the soundness of the report.

It is also said that this restraint took place on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. Imam Abu Hanifah cited, as evidence, the words of the verse "after He had given you victory over them," on the basis of this view, for the conquest of Makkah by force ('anwatan). The aforementioned view and the citing of the verse on its basis have been objected to. As for the first, the verse was revealed before the Conquest of Makkah. It has been replied that if what is meant is that it was revealed in its entirety before that, this is not established; rather some reports indicate otherwise. Otherwise it is of no benefit. Moreover, it is possible that this is a report of the unseen, as has been said of other verses of the surah. As for the second, its indication of force is disputed, for al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-fath is the gaining of victory over a thing, whether by force or by treaty. The difference between gaining victory over something and gaining victory by it lies in dominance, and that is present here, because they made a treaty while compelled, whereas the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him were free to choose." There is a subtle weakness in this that is not hidden, and likewise in what was objected to regarding the first point. In sum, this view, and likewise the citing of what is in the verse as evidence on its basis, is not a far-fetched construction. However, most of the sound reports, and what follows them, support what we said at first in the interpretation (tafsir) of the verse.

"And Allah is ever, of what you do" — of your deeds, or of everything you do, among which is pardoning after victory — "All-Seeing," so He will recompense you for it.

Abu 'Amr recited "ya'malun" with the third-person prefix, in which case the speech in it is a threat to the disbelievers.

﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque﴾, from reaching it and circumambulating it. ﴿And the offering﴾ in the accusative is in coordination (ʿaṭf) with the object pronoun in ﴿barred you﴾, meaning: and they barred the offering, which is what is brought as a gift to the House. Al-Akhfash said: its singular is hadyah, and for the female one is said hady, as if it were a verbal noun described by it. In al-Bahr it is stated that the sukūn of its dāl (hady) is the dialect of Quraysh, and the majority (al-Jumhūr) recited with it. Ibn Hurmuz, al-Ḥasan, ʿIṣmah from ʿĀṣim, al-Lu'lu'ī, and Kharijah from Abū ʿAmr recited with a kasrah on the dāl and a shaddah on the yā', and that is a dialect. It is on the pattern faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl, as more than one scholar has stated explicitly. This offering, according to what is well known, was seventy camels; Muqatil said it was one hundred camels. Al-Juʿfī from Abū ʿAmr recited (al-hadyi) in the genitive, as a coordination with ﴿the Sacred Mosque﴾ by deleting the governed noun, i.e., and the slaughter of the offering. It was also read in the nominative, on the assumption of an elided ﴿and the barring of the offering﴾. His words ﴿detained﴾ (maʿkūfan) are a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from (al-hadya) according to all the readings. It has been said that on the reading of the nominative it is permissible for (al-hadyu) to be a mubtadaʾ (subject), and the sentence would be like ḥukmuka masmaṭan (the phrase is uncertain). His words, may He be exalted: (wa-naḥnu ʿuṣbah, "while we are a band"), on the reading of the accusative, and that is as you see. The maʿkūf is the one held back. It is said: ʿakaftu al-rajula ʿan ḥājatihi (I held the man back from his need), I restrained him from it. Abū ʿAlī denied that ʿakafa takes a direct object, but Ibn Sīdah, al-Azharī and others related it. The apparent meaning of what is in the verse is

[p. 113 continued] with them. His words, may He be exalted, ﴿that it reach its place﴾ (an yablugha maḥillahu), are a badal al-ishtimāl (substitution of inclusion) from (al-hadya), as if it were said: and they barred the reaching of the offering to its place, or they barred from the reaching of the offering, or and he barred the reaching of the offering, according to the variation of the readings. It is also permitted that it be an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi) for the barring, i.e., out of dislike that it reach its place. And it is permitted that it be a mafʿūl min ajlihi in the genitive with an implied lām, for (maʿkūfan), i.e., detained for the sake of its reaching its place, and the detention would be by the Muslims. And it is permitted that it be in the accusative by removing the preposition, which is either min or ʿan, i.e., detained from or away from its reaching its place, in which case the detention is by the polytheists, as is the apparent sense. The maḥall (place) of the offering is the location where its slaughter becomes lawful, i.e., where it is permitted, or the place of its alighting, i.e., its obligation and occurrence, as is related from al-Zamakhsharī. The intended place is the known one, which is Minā. As for the view of al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, the place of it is for whoever is prevented wherever he is prevented, so it has reached its place in relation to the Prophet (ﷺ) and those with him, and therefore they slaughtered there, namely at al-Ḥudaybiyyah. As for the view of Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah be pleased with him, its place is the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram) in general, and part of al-Ḥudaybiyyah is within the Ḥaram according to him. They have related that the tents of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were outside of it, and his place of prayer was within the Ḥaram, and the slaughter occurred in what is within the Ḥaram; thus the offering reached its place without being detained from reaching it. Therefore the intended meaning must be the known place in order for that to be consistent. Al-Zamakhsharī claimed that the verse is evidence for Abū Ḥanīfah that the prohibited place of the offering is the Ḥaram, then he spoke in a manner whose defect is not hidden from one who examines it. Some people argued for the inference that al-Masjid al-Ḥarām may mean the Ḥaram, and that when they barred them from it and prevented their offering from entering so that it might reach its place, this indicates by apparent sense that it is its place. Then he said: and it does not contradict this that he (peace be upon him) slaughtered in a part of it, just as the barring from it does not contradict the fact that his place of prayer (peace be upon him) was within it, because they prevented them but did not completely forbid them. And that is as you see. But the fairness is that the inference from the verse for this claim does not hold at all. Some eminent Shāfiʿī scholars disputed that any part of al-Ḥudaybiyyah is within the Ḥaram, and said: it is contrary to what the majority hold, and the boundaries of the Ḥaram have been known since the time of Abraham (peace be upon him). No account is to be relied upon which al-Wāqidī corrupted, how much less when al-Bukhārī has explicitly stated in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from trustworthy narrators, the opposite; and the narration from al-Zuhrī is not authentic. End of quotation. Perhaps the one who said that part of it is within the Ḥaram based that on a sound report. Among their principles is that the affirmer is given precedence over the negator. And Allah knows best.

﴿And were it not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know﴾: the description of (men and women) is by the predominance of the masculine over the feminine. According to what Abū Nuʿaym related with a good chain, and others, from Abū Jumuʿah Jundub ibn Sabuʿ, they were nine persons: seven men, of whom he was one, and two women. His words, may He be exalted, ﴿that you should trample them﴾ (an taṭaʾūhum) is a badal al-ishtimāl from them. It is permitted that it be a badal from the object pronoun in ﴿you did not know them﴾, but Abū Ḥayyān considered this unlikely. The waṭʾ (trampling) is the treading down, and it is here used metaphorically for destruction. This is a fine metaphor, found in their speech both in ancient and modern times. Among that is the saying of al-Ḥārith ibn Waʿlah al-Dhuhlī:

"And she trampled us with a trampling in anger, / the trampling of a chained one, a grey-haired one with the old age of his prime"

And the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a ḥadīth: "Indeed the last trampling that Allah trampled was at Wajj."

And his (ﷺ) saying: "O Allah, press down Your trampling upon Muḍar."

﴿Then there would befall you from them﴾, i.e., from their direction, ﴿a maʿarrah﴾, i.e., a disliked thing and a hardship, taken from al-ʿArr and al-ʿArrah, which is the stubborn, persistent mange. More than one scholar said: it is a mafʿalah from ʿarrahu, when something disliked overtakes and befalls him. What is meant by it here, according to what is related from Mundhir ibn Saʿīd, is the reproach of the disbelievers and their saying about the believers: they have killed the people of their own religion. It has also been said: it is grief over them and the soul's pain at what befell them. Ibn Zayd said: it is the sin for killing them. Ibn Isḥāq said: it is the blood-money (diyah). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: both views are weak, because there is neither sin nor blood-money for killing a believer whose faith is concealed among the people of war. Al-Ṭabarī said: it is the expiation (kaffārah). Some have objected to this also, saying that the obligation of expiation is a matter of disagreement among the jurists. In al-Fuṣūl al-ʿImādiyyah there is a mention, in establishing analogous principles in jurisprudence, that our companions said: the abode of war prevents the obligation of what is averted by doubts, because our rulings do not apply in their abode, and the ruling of their abode does not apply in our abode. According to al-Shāfiʿī, the abode of war does not prevent the obligation of what is averted by doubts. The explanation of that: a combatant who embraced Islam in the abode of war and killed a Muslim who had entered their abode under safe conduct, there is no retaliation (qiṣāṣ) against him according to us, nor blood-money; but according to al-Shāfiʿī there is retaliation against him. On this basis, if two Muslims who were in agreement entered the abode of war and one killed the other, there is no retaliation against him according to us, but according to al-Shāfiʿī he is liable to that. Then he mentioned a matter in which Abū Ḥanīfah, Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad differed, and said: if one of two captives kills his companion in the abode of war, there is nothing against him according to Abū Ḥanīfah and Abū Yūsuf except the expiation, because he is a follower of theirs, and so he became like one of the people of war. According to Muḥammad, blood-money is obligatory, because he has the status of his own self, so the ruling for his self is considered separately. End of quotation. It is related from al-Kāfī that whoever embraced Islam in the abode of war and did not migrate to us, and a Muslim killed him intentionally or by mistake, and he has Muslim heirs, then [if it was intentional] he is liable for nothing, and if it was by mistake he is liable for the expiation but not the blood-money. End of quotation. The complete discussion of this matter is sought in its proper place. Al-Zamakhsharī explained the maʿarrah as the obligation of blood-money and expiation, and the evil speech of the polytheists, and the sin if some negligence proceeded from them; and that is as we see.

﴿Without knowledge﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the addressees in ﴿you trample them﴾. It has been said there is no repetition with his words ﴿you did not know them﴾, whether ﴿that you trample them﴾ is a badal al-ishtimāl from (men and women), or a badal from the accusative in ﴿you did not know them﴾. As for the second, the meaning comes to: and were it not for believers, you would not have known their trampling and destruction, while you did not know them to be believers, because the possibility that they would be destroyed without awareness despite their faith is the cause of restraint, so two kinds of knowledge are required in it. The object of knowledge in the first is the trampling, and in the second it is themselves in terms of their faith. As for the first, since His words, may He be exalted, ﴿without knowledge﴾ are a ḥāl from the subject of ﴿you trample them﴾, the knowledge concerning them returns to knowledge regarding the destruction, as you say: I destroyed him without knowledge, so neither is the destruction without awareness nor is knowledge of their faith attained; and both matters, being intended in themselves, are explicitly stated, even if they are close or mutually implicating in general. It is permitted to take ﴿you did not know them﴾ as a metaphor for mixing, as the words of al-Kashshāf hint, and this too removes the repetition; and there is a discussion of that which is resolved by reflection. It is also permitted that it be a ḥāl from the pronoun of (from them), or that it be connected to (you would be struck by), or an adjective of (maʿarrah). It has been said: the meaning is: there would befall you from them a maʿarrah without knowledge from the one who reproaches you and blames you, meaning if you trampled them not knowing, there would attach to you a disgrace from the disbelievers without knowledge, i.e., they would not know that you are excused in it; or the meaning is: you did not know that you were trampling them, so there would befall you from them a maʿarrah without knowledge from you, i.e., you would kill them without knowledge from you, or harm them without knowledge. So understand this and do not be heedless. The answer to (were it not for) is omitted, because the speech indicates it, and the meaning according to what you heard first: were it not for the dislike that you destroy people who are believers among the disbelievers, unaware of them, so that there would befall you by their destruction a disliked thing, He would have restrained your hands from them. The sum of it is that He, Exalted, even had He not restrained your hands from them, the matter would have led to the destruction of believers among them, so there would befall you from that a disliked thing, and He, Mighty and Majestic, dislikes that.

Ibn Jurayj said: Allah repelled the polytheists at al-Ḥudaybiyyah by means of people from among the Muslims who were among them. The apparent sense of the first, as has been said, is that the reason for the restraint is the protection of the addressees from incurring the maʿarrah, and the apparent sense of this is that its reason is the protection of those believers from being trampled, and the matter in that is easy. His words, may He be exalted, ﴿that Allah may admit into His mercy﴾ are a reason for what the omitted answer indicates, according to what he chose in al-Irshād; as if it were said: but He, glorified, restrained them from them so that by that restraint, which led to the conquest without any harm, He might admit into His vast mercy ﴿whom He wills﴾, and they are those believers. That [is realized] through their security, the removal of their weakness under the hands of the polytheists, and through their being granted success to establish the rites of worship in the most complete manner. Expressing them as (whom He wills) rather than with a pronoun, such as "that Allah may admit them into His mercy," is to indicate that the reason for admission is the will founded upon manifold wisdoms and interests. Some have made it a reason for what is understood from the protection of the believers in Mecca; and mercy means granting them success in increasing goodness and obedience by preserving them in their deeds and obedience. It is also permitted that by (whom He wills) is meant some of the polytheists, and by mercy is meant Islam, for when those believers were protected by the mentioned restraint, they displayed their faith because of witnessing the strength of the religion, so those who were heading toward Islam would follow them. Some have approved its being a reason for the restraint that is justified by protection.

It is also permitted that by (whom He wills) is meant the believers, so mercy means the granting of success for increase in goodness; and the disbelievers, so mercy means Islam. He explained the reason with the statement that when they witnessed the prevention of their punishment after victory over them, because of the mingling of believers with them out of concern for their affair, they desired Islam and joining the rank of those shown mercy; and that when the believers knew of the prevention of the punishment of the polytheists after victory over them because of their mingling with them, they displayed their faith so that they would be followed. He said: there is no reason to make the lām figurative from the meaning of causation for what results from a thing, because that is a departure from the immediate literal meaning without a motive. As for what is supposed, that the causation of the restraint by what has been mentioned, along with its being caused by protection, is invalid because it involves two causes for one individual effect, this is invalid because when causes are not fully complete in reality, their plurality does no harm, and what is here is of that kind.

This is the further part of al-Alusi's discussion, and in my view it is better to take that as the cause of what the answer indicates, as you heard earlier, because of the tight coherence of the noble composition. Taking (whom He wills) to refer to the oppressed believers, and not to some of the polytheists, is more fitting with His words, exalted is He: ﴿Had they been separated, We would have punished those among them who disbelieved with a painful punishment﴾. Tazayyul means separation and distinction. It is also permitted that the pronoun in ﴿tazayyalū﴾ refers to the believers mentioned earlier, meaning: had those believing men and believing women separated and distinguished themselves from the disbelievers and left Makkah, and not remained among them, We would have punished, etc. It is also permitted that it refers to the believers and the disbelievers together, meaning: had some of them separated from others and not remained mixed, We would have punished, etc.

Many have chosen the first view. For them, (li) is for explanation, and what is meant is their punishment in this world by killing and captivity, as Mujahid and others said; otherwise (law) would have no function. The clause is a resumptive clause confirming what precedes it. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that His words, ﴿Had they been separated﴾, be like a repetition of His words (Had it not been for men [who are believers]), since their meaning is one thing, and that "we would have punished" is the answer of the earlier (lawla). Abu Hayyan objected that the difference is evident, so it is not a repetition nor like one. It was answered that the reluctance to trample them because they could not be distinguished from the disbelievers, which is the meaning of the second, makes it a kind of substitution of inclusion, and that suffices for it to be like a repetition. Ibn al-Munir said: their reference is one even though (lawla) indicates the prevention of something due to the existence of something, while (law) indicates the prevention of something due to the prevention of something else. Between these two there is an evident contrast, because (lawla) here governs an existence, and (law) governs ﴿tazayyalū﴾, which refers back to the non-existence of their being; the prevention of non-existence is an affirmation, so both return to one matter from this angle. He said: My grandfather used to prefer this view and call it tatriyah (renewal), and it occurs most often when the discourse grows long and the earlier part is distant, and the later part needs to be built upon the earlier, so sometimes it renews it with the same wording and sometimes with different wording that conveys the same meaning. End of quote.

You know that in the omission of the answer there is evidence of the intensity of God's wrath, and that were it not for the rights of the believers He would have done to them what does not fall under description and cannot be measured. From this it is known that this view is preferable to making ﴿tazayyalū﴾ serve as a repetition for the sake of renewal, so renewing and strengthening the answer is better and more suited to the requirement of the context. Al-Tibi also chose the first view, giving as his reason that it then comes close to the category of exclusion and inversion (al-tard wal-'aks), since the implied meaning is: were it not for the existence of believers mingled with the polytheists and not distinguished from them, there would have befallen them what was the recompense for their disbelief and obstruction; and were distinction achieved and mixing removed, the punishment would have occurred. Furthermore, the estimate of the answer as mentioned earlier, according to those who hold the omission, is what many have adopted. Some permitted estimating it as: "He would have hastened for them what they deserve," and took His words, ﴿They are those who disbelieved﴾, etc., as if it were said: "They are those who disbelieved and deserved hastening in their destruction; and were it not for believing men, etc., He would have hastened that for them." This is also better than the view of repetition.

Ibn Abi Abla, Ibn Miqsam, Abu Haywah and Ibn 'Awn read (lau tazayalū) on the pattern of tafā'alū.

In the verse, according to what al-Kiya said, there is evidence that it is not permitted to breach the ship of the disbelievers if there are Muslim captives in it, and likewise to shell fortresses when they are in them and the disbelievers use them as shields. There is discussion of this in the books of jurisprudence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 26 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When those who disbelieved set in their hearts zealotry (ḥamiyyah)﴾ is in the accusative governed by "remember" (udhkur) as an object, or by "We punished" (ʿadhdhabnā) as a temporal adverb, or by "they barred you" (ṣaddūkum) in the same manner. It has also been said that it is governed by a hidden verb—may God Most High be gracious to you. Whatever the case, "those who" (alladhīna) is the subject of "set" (jaʿala). Placing the relative pronoun in the position of their pronoun serves to censure them by what is contained in the relative clause, and to give the reason for the ruling by it. The verb "set" (jaʿala) is either in the sense of "casting" (al-ilqāʾ), so God Most High's words ﴿in their hearts﴾ are connected to it; or in the sense of "making" (al-taṣyīr), in which case it is connected to a omitted element that is its second object, meaning: they made zealotry firmly established in their hearts. Because it was acquired by them in some respect, its setting was attributed to them. Al-Naysaburi said:

It is permissible that the subject of "set" be the pronoun of God Most High, and "in their hearts" is an explanation of the place of the setting, and the meaning becomes: when God set in the hearts of those who disbelieved zealotry—and that, as you see, is far-fetched. Ḥamiyyah is arrogance (al-anafah); it is said: "I was zealous about such-and-such" (ḥamaytu ʿan kadhā ḥamiyyatan) when I was too proud of it and shame came over me because of it.

Al-Raghib said: The irascible faculty, when it stirs up and grows strong, is expressed by ḥamiyyah, so it is said: "I was zealous against so-and-so," meaning I was angry with him. God Most High's words ﴿the zealotry of ignorance﴾ are an apposition to "zealotry," meaning the zealotry of the ignorant religion, or the zealotry arising from ignorance, because it is without proof and in other than its proper place. God Most High's words ﴿then God sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾ are coordinated with "set" (jaʿala), on the supposition that "when" (idh) is an object of "remember." The purpose is to remind of the good conduct of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, by God's granting success, and of the evil conduct of the polytheists. What the conditional clause indicates, if it is taken as a temporal adverb of "We punished," is as if it were said: "they did not separate, so We did not punish, then He sent down..." etc. It is also governed by a hidden verb operating on it in the last of the mentioned views, and this would be like an explanation of that. As for taking it as a temporal adverb of ﴿they barred you﴾, it is said the coordination is with "set," and it is said with ﴿they barred you﴾. It is like the saying "the bird is angry, so Zayd becomes angry at the fly." The best of these views is not hidden. Tranquillity (al-sakīnah) is calm assurance and gravity.

Many narrators reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) went out with those who were with him to al-Hudaybiyyah. When he reached Dhu al-Ḥulayfah, he garlanded the sacrificial animals, marked them, and entered the state of ihram for ʿumrah, and he sent ahead of him a scout from Khuzaʿah to inform him about the Quraysh. The Prophet (ﷺ) proceeded until he reached Ghadir al-Ashtat, near ʿUsfan. His scout came to him and said: "Indeed the Quraysh have gathered great forces against you, and they have gathered the Aḥābīsh against you. They will fight you and bar you from the House." He consulted the people about raiding the offspring of those who had helped them. Abu Bakr said: "God and His Messenger know best, O Prophet of God. We came only as ʿumrah pilgrims and did not come to fight anyone, but whoever stands between us and the House, we will fight him." The Prophet (ﷺ) said:
"Proceed in the name of God." So he proceeded until he halted at the furthest part of al-Hudaybiyyah. Budayl ibn Warqa' al-Khuzaʿi came to him with a group from his people and said to him: "I have left Kaʿb ibn Luʾay and ʿĀmir ibn Luʾay, who have encamped nearby with the milch camels with their young. They will fight you and bar you from the House." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We have not come to fight anyone, but as ʿumrah pilgrims. The Quraysh have been worn down by war and harmed by it. What would it cost them if they left me and the rest of the Arabs? If the Arabs kill me, that is what they wanted; and if God makes me prevail over them, they will enter Islam in multitudes. And if they do not do that, I will fight them while I have strength. What does the Quraysh think? By God, I will not cease to struggle against them for the sake of what God has sent me with, until God makes it prevail, or this matter is cut off." Budayl said: "I will convey to them what you say." He conveyed it to them. ʿUrwah ibn Masʿud al-Thaqafi said to them: "Let me go to him." He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him something similar to what he said to Budayl, and words passed between them, and he saw the respect the Companions showed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and their veneration of him, which he saw. He returned to his companions, informed them of that, and said: "Indeed he has offered you a course of right guidance, so accept it." A man from the Banu Kinanah said: "Let me go to him." When he drew near the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is so-and-so, and he is from a people who honor the sacrificial camels; send them to him." They were sent, and the people met him reciting the talbiyah. When he saw that, he said: "Glory be to God! It is not fitting that these be barred from the House." He returned and informed his companions. A man called Mukarraz ibn Hafs said: "Let me go to him." When he drew near, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is Mukarraz, and he is a wicked man." He began speaking with the Prophet (ﷺ), and while he was speaking, Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, brother of the Banu ʿAmir ibn Luʾay, came. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Your affair has been made easy for you." The Quraysh had sent him and said to him: "Go to Muhammad and make peace with him, and let there be in the peace only that he return from us this year. By God, the Arabs will never say that he entered it against us by force, ever." When he reached the Prophet (ﷺ), he spoke at length, and the matter ended in peace and the writing of a document to that effect. The Prophet (ﷺ) called ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, and said: "Write: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Suhayl said: "I do not know this; rather write: In your name, O God." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Write: In your name, O God." So he wrote it. Then he said: "Write: This is what Muhammad, Messenger of God, has agreed upon with Suhayl ibn ʿAmr." Suhayl said: "If we knew you were the Messenger of God, we would not have barred you from the House nor fought you. But write your name and your father's name." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By God, I am indeed the Messenger of God, even if you deny me. Write: This is what Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah has agreed upon with Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, a peace on laying down war from the people for ten years, in which people will be safe and some will refrain from others, on the condition that whoever comes to Muhammad from the Quraysh without the permission of his guardian, he shall return him to them; and whoever comes to the Quraysh from those with Muhammad, they will not return him to him. There is between us a closed chest, and there is no secret theft nor treachery. Whoever wishes to enter the covenant and pact of Muhammad may enter it, and whoever wishes to enter the covenant and pact of the Quraysh may enter it. Muhammad shall return from Makkah this year and not enter it; and when the coming year comes, the people of Makkah shall leave, and he shall enter it with his Companions and remain there three days, with the riders' weapons being swords in their sheaths, not entering with anything else."

The apparent meaning of this report is that Suhayl did not accept that Muhammad, Messenger of God, be written before he wrote [his own name]. It came in another narration that he wrote and did not accept it, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said to ʿAli, may God ennoble his face: "Erase it." He said: "I am not the one who will erase it." This came in a narration of al-Bukhari and Muslim. In another narration of al-Bukhari, in the Maghazi: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) took the document, while he did not know how to write, and wrote: This is what Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah has settled." Likewise al-Nasa'i and Ahmad related it, and its wording is: "He took the document, while he was not able to write, and wrote in place of 'Messenger of God': This is what Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah has settled."
