Abu al-Walid al-Baji adhered to the apparent meaning of this narration, as in Fath al-Bari, to hold that the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote after he had not been able to write, and his teacher Abu Dharr al-Harawi agreed with him in that, as did Abu al-Fath al-Naysaburi and others from the scholars of Ifriqiyyah. The majority hold that he (ﷺ) did not write, and that his saying "he took the document, while he was not able to write" is to explain that he needed ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, to show him the place of the word he refused to erase, because he did not know how to write. His saying "he wrote," by way of supposition, means "then he erased it," so he returned the document to ʿAli, who wrote; or the word "wrote" is used loosely for ordering writing. The full discussion is in its place.

So their zealotry, according to what al-Durr al-Manthur reports from a group, was that they did not acknowledge that he (ﷺ) was a Messenger, did not acknowledge [the formula] "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," and barred the Muslims from the House. The believers resolved to attack them for that, so God sent down His tranquillity upon them, and they became dignified and forbearing. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj, concerning "the zealotry of ignorance," that he said: "The Quraysh were zealous that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) should enter upon them, and they said: 'He shall never enter upon us.'" Ibn Bahr said, as in al-Bahr: their zealotry was their partisanship for their idols, and their disdain that they should worship other than them. In placing "upon" (ʿalā) between "the Messenger" and "the believers" there is an indication that He, glorified is He, sent down to each a tranquillity suited to him.

The reason for putting the sending down before the Messenger (ﷺ) is not hidden. Al-Imam said: In this verse there are subtle meanings: that God Most High made clear the utmost distance between the believers and the disbelievers, by distinguishing between the two agents—the subject of "set" is the disbelievers, and the subject of "sent down" is God Most High—and between the two objects, for that is zealotry and this is tranquillity; and between the two idafahs: the attribution of zealotry to ignorance, and the attribution of tranquillity to Him; and between the two verbs "set" and "sent down." Zealotry is set in the present circumstance like an accident that does not last, while tranquillity is like something preserved in the treasury of mercy, which He sent down. Zealotry is ugly and blameworthy in itself, and it became uglier by being attributed to ignorance; tranquillity is good in itself, and it became better by being attributed to God, Mighty and Majestic. The conjunction in "then sent down" with fa' rather than waw indicates reciprocity and recompense. You say: "Zayd honored me, so I honored him." So it indicates that the sending down of tranquillity was in return for their setting zealotry in their hearts, so that the believers did not become angry nor flee, but endured; and that is rare in custom, so it is from God's bounty, Most High. End of quotation, and it is not objectionable.

﴿And He made them hold fast to the word of piety﴾: it is "There is no god but God," as al-Tirmidhi, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, al-Daraqutni and others related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb with a raised (marfuʿ) chain; and as Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah and Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ likewise.

Ahmad, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim related from Humran that ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may God be pleased with him, said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed I know a word that no servant says truthfully from his heart except that he is forbidden to the Fire.'" ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said: "I will tell you what it is: it is the word of sincerity (kalimat al-ikhlas) which God, glorified is He, made Muhammad and his Companions hold fast to, and it is the word of piety (kalimat al-taqwa) upon which the Prophet of God (ﷺ) urged his uncle Abu Talib at death: the testimony that there is no god but God." This is also related from ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, as Abu Hayyan reported, and from Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Saʿid ibn Jubayr and others. ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related it from ʿAta' al-Khurasani with the addition "Muhammad is the Messenger of God." It is attributed to piety (al-taqwa) because by it shirk is guarded against; and from here Ibn ʿAbbas said, as Ibn al-Mundhir and others related: "It is the head of every piety." The apparent sense of ʿUmar's words, may God be pleased with him, is that the pronoun in "made them hold fast" (alzamahum) refers to the Messenger (ﷺ) and those with him, and their being made to hold fast to it was by ruling and ordering it.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and al-Hakim related it and graded it sound.

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* and a group of narrators report from ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, that he said: "It is *la ilaha illa Allah* and *Allahu akbar*." A similar report is also transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad* report from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah that he said: "It is *la ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah*." Ibn Abi Rabah and Mujahid also report that it is *la ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu al-mulk wa lahu al-hamd wa huwa ʿala kulli shay'in qadir*. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and others report from al-Zuhri that he said: "It is *bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim*." Some added to this *Muhammad rasul Allah*.

The meaning of "making them bind themselves to it" is that it was chosen for them, in preference to those who turned away from it to *bismika Allahumma* and *Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah*. It has also been said that the word (*kalimah*) means steadfastness and fulfilment of the covenant, and al-Khafaji attributed this to al-Hasan. Their being "bound" to it means being commanded to it. The use of the word *kalimah* for steadfastness in the covenant and for fulfilling it is said to be because each of them is a means of reaching the goal. This is similar to what has been said about applying the term *kalimah* to ʿIsa, peace be upon him, because each of them is a means of guidance. The genitive construction, on the view that the word means steadfastness, is taken as the construction of cause to effect, so it is an annexation of the slightest connection. It is also permissible that it be an exclusive, literal annexation, with an omitted noun, meaning "the word of the people of piety." By "covenant," according to what the apparent occasion of revelation requires, is meant the treaty of peace that took place between him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and the people of Makkah. It has also been said that it includes that and all their other covenants with him, may He be exalted and glorified.

You know that the view mentioned is not, in itself, apparent. Similar to it is what has been said: the word refers to their statement in the loins, "Yes," acknowledging His oneness, may His majesty be exalted, and "binding" means commanding steadfastness and fulfilment of it. It has also been said that it is the saying of the believers, "We hear and obey," when they are commanded or forbidden. The apparent reading of this is that the pronoun refers to the believers. The most preponderant of the views on this word is what has been transmitted as a prophetic statement (*marfuʿan*), and it is the view taken by the great majority. What is mentioned in the earlier reports is probably by way of brevity, and the intended meaning is *la ilaha illa Allah Muhammad rasul Allah*.

*Wa kanu* is coordinated with what precedes it, or is a circumstantial clause for the object in *alzamahum*, with *qad* assumed or not. The apparent reference of the pronoun is, as with the preceding one, to the Messenger and the believers, as the words of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, indicate. Some have preferred that it refers only to the believers, and it seems that they regarded the first pronoun as also referring to them, which is not objectionable. Perhaps they took the nearer antecedent as the basis. So the meaning is: "The believers were, in the knowledge of Allah, ﴿more deserving of it﴾," that is, of the word of piety. The elative form (*afʿal*) denotes an increase in the deservingness of the thing itself, that is, they are characterized by a greater claim to it. Or, according to what is most commonly held about it, the standard of comparison is omitted, meaning "more deserving of it than the disbelievers of Makkah," because Allah chose them for His religion and for the companionship of His Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. It has been said that the comparison is with the Jews and Christians, and it has been said with all nations, because they are "the best nation brought forth for mankind."

Al-Mubarrad reported that the earlier peoples could say *la ilaha illa Allah* only once in a day and night, and none of them could say it more than that. The one who said it would stretch out his voice with it until his breath gave out, out of blessing through the mention of Allah, may He be exalted. Allah, may He be mighty and glorified, has made it possible for this community to say it whenever they wish. This is His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And He made them bind themselves to the word of piety﴾, meaning He urged them to mention it as much as they could, and they were more deserving of it. This report has not been established. Al-Imam permitted that the comparison be with respect to other than the word of piety, meaning "more deserving of it than a word other than the word of piety," and he said: "This is like your saying, 'Zayd is more deserving of honour than of humiliation,' and your saying, when a person is asked about Zayd, whether he is more knowledgeable in medicine or in jurisprudence: 'Zayd is more knowledgeable in jurisprudence,' meaning than in medicine." In this there is an oversight that is not hidden. ﴿And its people﴾, that is, those who are fit for it, and this is more emphatic than "more deserving." So much so that it has been said that the difference between them is like the difference between *al-ahaqq* (more deserving) and *al-haqq* (the truth). It has also been said that their being more deserving of it than the disbelievers implies that they are superior to them in some degree, but does not establish fitness, just as when a king chooses two people for a task, and each of them is not suitable for it, but one of them is further from being entitled to it. Then it is said of the nearer of the two, if one of them must be chosen, "This one is more deserving," just as one says, "Imprisonment is less severe than execution." To prevent the misunderstanding of such a thing in the matter at hand, He, may He be glorified, said: ﴿and its people﴾. It has also been said that the meaning is that they are more deserving of it in this world, and its people for reward in the Hereafter. It has also been said that there is an inversion in the verse, and the original order was "They were its people and more deserving of it." Likewise it reads so in the *mushaf* (codex) of al-Harith ibn Suwayd, the companion of Ibn Masʿud, who was the one whose codex was buried for opposing the Imam in the days of al-Hajjaj. He was among the senior and trustworthy Successors of Kufa. It has also been said that the pronoun in *kanu* refers to the disbelievers of Makkah, meaning: "Those disbelievers who placed zealotry in their hearts were more deserving of the word of piety, because they are the people of the Sacred Sanctuary of Allah, and among them was His Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and his warning to them has already been mentioned, were it not that they were deprived of success." There is in this what there is, whether the pronoun of *alzamahum* is also taken to refer to the disbelievers of Makkah or not. I suspect in its proponent a Rafidi (Shiʿi extremist) inclination that led him to it, but his purpose is not achieved by it. It has also been said that the pronoun in *kanu* refers to the believers, except that the two pronouns in ﴿with it and its people﴾ refer to tranquillity. There is in this a departure from the apparent meaning without any need. It has also been said that both refer to Makkah, meaning: "They were more deserving of entering Makkah, and its people." The mention of Makkah brings to mind the Sacred Mosque in His statement: ﴿and they barred you from the Sacred Mosque﴾, and likewise the place of sacrifice in His statement, may He be glorified: ﴿and the offering held back from reaching its place of sacrifice﴾. There is in this what is not hidden. ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing of all things﴾, so He, may He be glorified, knows the right of everything and its fitness for what it deserves, and so He, may He be mighty and glorified, drives the right to its rightful recipient and the one who is fit to its fitting one. Or, He knows this, and He knows what wisdom and benefit require of sending down tranquillity and being content with the treaty. Thus this serves as a concluding statement for everything that came before.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 27:

﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled His Messenger's vision.﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw in a dream, before he set out for al-Hudaybiyyah, that he and his companions had entered Makkah in safety, having shaved their heads and cut short their hair. He related the vision to his companions, and they rejoiced and were glad. They supposed that they would enter it in that same year, and they said: "The vision of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is true." When that was delayed, Abdullah ibn Ubayy, Abdullah ibn Nufayl and Rifa'ah ibn al-Harith objected, saying: "By Allah, we did not shave our heads, we did not cut short our hair, and we did not see the Sacred Mosque." Then this verse was revealed. It is also narrated from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said something similar, by way of seeking clarification so that his certainty might increase. In another report, the vision of the Prophet (ﷺ) was only that a king came to him and said: "You will surely enter..." and so on. The meaning is: Allah, glorified is He, fulfilled His Messenger's vision, and this is of the type of omission and transitivity, as in the saying: "The age of the she-camel made me true (ṣadaqanī sinnu bakrihi)." Its realization is that He, exalted is He, showed him a true vision.

Al-Raghib said: truthfulness (al-ṣidq) can be by speech and by action, and what is in the verse is truthfulness by action, which is realization; that is, He, glorified is He, made His vision come true. In al-Kirmani's commentary, it is said: "kadhaba" takes two objects, as in "kadhabanī al-ḥadīth" (he made me a liar regarding the report), and similarly "ṣadaqa" as in the verse. This is strange, since the heavier form (ṣaddaqa) takes one object and the lighter form (ṣadaqa) takes two objects, the end of the quotation. In al-Bahr: "ṣadaqa" takes two objects, the second of which is governed either directly or by a preposition; you say: "ṣadaqtu Zaydan al-ḥadīth" and "ṣadaqtuhu fī al-ḥadīth." Some have counted it among the verbs like "istaghfara" and "amara." The well-known view is what we indicated at first. (*bi-al-ḥaqq*) is an adjunct to an omitted verbal noun, that is, truthfulness accompanied by the truth, i.e., by the correct decree and the far-reaching wisdom, which is the manifestation of the state of the one who is shaken in faith and the one who is firm in it. For this reason, the realization of the vision was delayed until the following year. Or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a state qualifying the action) from the vision, i.e., accompanied by the truth, not among the confused dreams (aḍghāth al-aḥlām). It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the Glorious Name, or from (*rasūlahu*). It is also permitted that it be an adverbial complement (ẓarf laghw) of "ṣadaqa," or that it be an oath by al-Ḥaqq, which is among His names, mighty and majestic, or by the opposite of falsehood. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ is the answer to the oath. The pause is on (*al-ru'yā*), and this, in all that has preceded, is the answer to an implied oath. The pause is on (*bi-al-ḥaqq*), meaning: By Allah, you will surely enter, and so on. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿if Allah wills﴾ makes the promise conditional upon the will, to teach the servants. With this, the objection is resolved which says: He, exalted is He, is the Creator of all things and knows them before they occur, so how does the conditional occur from Him, glorified is He, with the will? In the sense of what has been mentioned is the statement of Tha'lab: He, glorified and exalted is He, made an exception regarding what He knows, so that creatures may make exceptions regarding what they do not know.

In this is an allusion that the occurrence of the entering is from His will, exalted is He, not from their own vigour and planning. Al-Khafaji mentioned that the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun, and the original is: "You will surely enter it without doubt, unless He wills the non-entering." It is then a promise to them, turned away from its apparent sense for the sake of an allusion to them and a rebuke to those who objected to the vision, so it is of the type of metonymy (kināya). The end of the quotation. The question has also been answered in other ways, and it was said: The doubt returns to the addressees. And there is something in this which you will know soon, if Allah wills. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said:

[Page 121]

The conditional returns to the entering of all of them. This is related from al-Jubba'i. It was also said: it refers to safety, so it is a displacement from its place (taqdīm min ta'khīr), that is, "You will surely enter it while you are ﴿in security﴾ from the enemy, if Allah wills." Al-Zamakhshari rejected both views in al-Kashshaf, saying: As for making the conditional the qualifier of their entering as captives or in safety, the question remains, because the specific entering is also a report from Allah, exalted is He, and it contradicts doubt. It is not like the saying of Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security﴾, since it is not unlikely that he, peace be upon him, did not know the outcome of the matter as to safety or fear. So it should either be interpreted as the doubt returning to the addressees, or as a teaching. The second is preferable, because giving precedence to those who doubt does not suit this context; rather the matter is the reverse. As for the answer to the objection to al-Husayn, it is that the meaning is that it is equivalent to: "Those whom Allah wills to enter from among you will surely enter it," so it is a metonymy for the fact that some of them will not enter it, because their term prevents them from it. Thus there is no need to return to what has been mentioned.

It was also said: it is a quotation of what the angel of the vision said to him (ﷺ), and this is the view of Ibn Kaysan. Or it is a quotation of what he himself, peace and blessings be upon him, said to his companions. This was rejected by the author of al-Taqrib, saying: How can something that is not part of His speech enter into His speech without a quotation? It was answered that the meaning is that the answer to the oath is an explanation of the vision; the speaker of it in the dream was the angel, and in waking life it was the Messenger (ﷺ). So it is in the status of what is reported, when examined closely, as if it were said: "It is the saying of the angel or the Messenger: 'You will surely enter...'" You know that this, though it corrects the noble arrangement, does not remove the remoteness. Al-Zamakhshari objected to this, but he claimed that its being a quotation of what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said is less remote than making it the saying of the angel.

Abu Ubayda and a group of grammarians said: (*in*) means (*idh*, "when"), and they cited as an example His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will be superior if you are believers﴾, and his (ﷺ) saying when visiting graves: "You are the forerunners, and we, if Allah wills, will surely join you."

The Basrans do not accept this. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿shaving your heads and cutting short (your hair)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) like "in security," from the omitted waw, because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, from His saying: ﴿You will surely enter﴾. However, "in security" is a concomitant circumstance (ḥāl muqārana), while this is a future circumstance (ḥāl muqaddara), because the entering is in the state of ihram, not in the state of shaving and cutting short. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "in security," and the meaning is: some of you shaving the heads of others, and others cutting short. So there is either an implied element in the speech, or there is the attribution of what belongs to a part to the whole. The evidence for this is that shaving and cutting short cannot be combined, and shaving is well known, while cutting short is taking some of the hair; so each of them must be attributed to some of them. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿without fear﴾ is also a circumstantial clause from the doer of ﴿You will surely enter﴾, to clarify the safety after the completion of the pilgrimage. "In security" earlier clarifies the safety at the time of entering. So there is no repetition. Or it is a circumstantial clause from the hidden pronoun in "in security." If by it the meaning of "in security" is intended, it is an emphatic circumstance (ḥāl mu'akkida). If it is intended as "without fear of blame for shaving or cutting short, and without loss of reward," then it is a circumstance that establishes a new meaning (ḥāl mu'assisa). The circumstance is clear if it is made a circumstance from the pronoun in ﴿shaving﴾ or ﴿cutting short﴾. It is also permitted that it be an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayānī, a new clause answering an implied question), in answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What then is the state after entering?" So it was said: "Without fear," that is, after entering.

The verse has been used as evidence that shaving is not required in the rite, but cutting short suffices in its place. The apparent sense of placing shaving before cutting short is that it is better, and this is what the reports indicate for other than women.

Al-Shaykhan, Ahmad and Ibn Majah narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, forgive those who shave." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, and those who cut short?" He said: "O Allah, forgive those who shave," three times. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, and those who cut short?" He said: "And those who cut short."

As for women, Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no shaving for women; for women there is only cutting short."

The Sunnah in shaving is that one begins with the right side. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated "from Anas that he saw the Prophet (ﷺ) say to the barber, 'Like this,' and he indicated with his hand the right side, and let him reach the two bones (of the head)," as Ata' said.

Ibn Abi Shaybah also narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them) that they used to say to the barber: "Begin with the right, and take the shaving down to the two bones."

The verse has also been used as evidence that cutting short applies to the head only, not to the beard or the rest of the body's hair, since the apparent meaning is: "and cutting short your heads," that is, their hair, since it is evident that the heads themselves are not cut short. ﴿So He knew what you did not know﴾. The apparent sense is that it is coordinated with ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled﴾. The order is by way of the actual connection to the known: that is, He knew, immediately after showing him the true vision, what you did not know of the wisdom motivating the advancement of what bears witness to the truth, as a practical knowledge. It was also said: the fa' indicates the order of mention. ﴿So He made, for the sake of this knowledge,﴾ ﴿besides that﴾, that is, besides the realization of the fulfilment of what He showed him of entering the Sacred Mosque in safety, and so on. It was also said: that is, besides the conquest of Makkah. The first is more evident, and this is more suitable to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a near victory﴾, which is the conquest of Khaybar, as Ibn Zayd and others said. What is meant by His making it is His promise and its fulfilment without delay, so that it may be taken as evidence of the truth of the vision, and so that the hearts of the believers may find comfort in the ease of its occurrence.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: ﴿what you did not know﴾ means the wisdom in delaying the conquest of Makkah until the following year. In this there are two matters. First, the conquest of Makkah did not occur in the year in which it was said, but in the eighth year; the figurative use of "the following year," or the interpretation of the conquest as the entry of the believers into Makkah as pilgrims, is untenable. Second, the fa' is incompatible with what has been mentioned, because His knowledge of that is definitely prior to the showing of the vision.

It was answered to this by upholding that the fa' indicates the order of mention, or that what is meant is: "He made manifest to you what He knew, which is the wisdom," so reflect.

It has been related from many of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) that the near victory in the verse is the Pledge of Ridwan. Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq said: it is the conquest of al-Hudaybiyyah. Among the strange views is that what is meant by it is the conquest of Makkah, although the Messenger (peace be upon him) and his companions did not enter it at that time. Moreover, this contradicts the context, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 28:

﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance﴾, meaning, accompanied by it. The bāʾ (the preposition "with") here expresses accompaniment, and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the object. His being accompanied by guidance means that he is a guide. It was also said: meaning, accompanied by the guidance. What is meant by guidance is the clear proof and the shining argument, or the Qur'an. It is also permissible for the bāʾ to indicate causation or purpose, and these two are close in meaning. The prepositional phrase is then connected to "sent," meaning, He sent him because of the guidance or for its sake. ﴿And the religion of truth﴾, and the religion of Islam. The apparent meaning is that it includes both the fundamentals (uṣūl, the core principles of belief) and the branches (furūʿ, the practical rulings). It is also permissible that "guidance" refers to the fundamentals and "the religion of truth" refers to the branches, since some of the Messengers, peace be upon them, were not sent with branch rulings but only with the fundamentals and their clarification. The apparent meaning of "the truth" is its opposite, falsehood. It is also permissible that it refers to one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, meaning, the religion of Allah, which is the Truth. The Imam (al-Razi) also allowed other interpretations. ﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾, that He may make it superior to the whole category of religion in all its forms, meaning, every system that is followed, including the laws and creeds. This includes both truth and falsehood. The original meaning of ižhār (making something prevail) is placing a thing on the back, so it is used as a metaphor for elevating it and for making it visible to the onlooker. Then the usage spread until it became a conventional meaning. Its prevailing over the truth is by abrogating (naskh, the removal of a ruling by a later revelation) some of its rulings that change with the changing of ages, and its prevailing over falsehood is by clarifying its falsity. Many scholars have also allowed, and this is perhaps the most apparent in context, that its prevailing over religion means the Muslims being empowered over all the adherents of the religions.
[Page 123]
They said: No people of a religion have fought the Muslims without the Muslims subduing them. It is sufficient for this that what has been mentioned has continued for a considerable period, as is not hidden from those who are acquainted with the books of history and events. It was also said: the full completion of this elevation will occur at the descent of ʿIsā (Jesus), peace be upon him, and the emergence of al-Mahdi, may Allah be pleased with him, when no religion will remain except Islam. The occurrence of the opposite of this afterward does not harm, either for something like what you have heard, or because what remains of the world at that time is a mere trifle. In general, there is an emphasis on what Allah, the Exalted, promised of conquest, and a settling of the hearts of the believers that He, the Exalted, will open for them of the lands and grant them such dominance over the regions that they will be able to manage them, namely the conquest of Makkah. ﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾, that what He, the Mighty and Majestic, has counted of making His religion prevail over all religions, or of the conquest, is certain to happen. Or: Allah suffices as a witness to His messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, because he claimed prophethood and Allah manifested a miracle at his hand, and that is a testimony from Him, the Exalted, to it. Al-Razi restricted himself to this interpretation and made it a consolation for what occurred from Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, when he refused to accept the writing of ﴿"Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah"﴾ and said what he said.

Some eminent scholars held that the manifestation of a miracle is also a testimony from Him, the Mighty and Majestic, to the fulfillment of His promise. It becomes apparent only when his, peace and blessings be upon him, report of it is added.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 48, verse 29 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Muhammadun Rasulullah﴾ That is, he is, or that is, the Messenger sent with guidance and the religion of truth. "Muhammad" is, according to the view that the noble name is the predicate of an omitted subject, and "Rasulullah" is an appositive (ʿatf bayan), or a qualifier (naʿt), or a substitute (badal). The sentence is a resumptive (istinaf) explanation of His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger﴾. This is the most preferred view and the most suitable to the context, as in al-Kashshaf. It is supported, considering some of the views that will come, God willing, by the reading of Ibn ʿAmir in one narration, "Rasula" (رَسُولَ) in the accusative, as a expression of praise (madh). His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And those who are with him﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is His, the Glorified, saying: ﴿are severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾.

Abu Hayyan said: The apparent view is that ﴿Muhammadun Rasulullah﴾ is a subject and predicate, and the sentence based on this is an explanation of what is witnessed to. As for the case where it is the Messengership, this is clear. As for the case where it is the fulfilment of the promise, it has been said: because the realisation of what He promised is necessarily tied to his being the Messenger of God, since he does not promise except what is certain, and does not report except what is wholly true.

It is also permitted that "Muhammad" be the subject, "wa-rasul" (and a messenger) be a follower of it, and "wa-alladhina maʿahu" (and those who are with him) be a conjunction (ʿatf) upon it, with the predicate about him and about them being His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿severe...﴾ etc.

Al-Hasan read ﴿ashidda'a﴾ and ﴿ruhama'a﴾ with the accusative for both. It was said that this is on the basis of praise (madh), and it was said on the basis of circumstance (hal). The governing element in both is the governing element in "maʿahu," so the predicate on this view is the clause ﴿tarahum﴾ which comes later. Likewise the predicate of "alladhina" on the first view. The intended meaning of "alladhina maʿahu" according to Ibn ʿAbbas is those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyah. Al-Jumhur said: all of his companions, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and God be pleased with them. "Ashidda'" is the plural of "shadid," and "ruhama'" is the plural of "rahim." The meaning is that among them is harshness and severity toward the enemies of the religion, and mercy and tenderness toward their fellow believers. In describing them with mercy after describing them with severity there is completion and a safeguard (ihtiras), for if he had been content with the first description, it might have been supposed that the implication of the restriction is not considered, and so harshness and roughness would be imagined absolutely. This is countered by appending the second description. The outcome is that they, while being severe against the enemies, are merciful toward their brothers. Similar to this is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾. On this basis is the saying of the poet:

Forbearing when forbearance adorns its people, yet before the enemy he is awe-inspiring.

It has reached us, as is reported from al-Hasan, that in their severity toward the disbelievers they were so careful that their garments would not touch the garments of the disbelievers, nor their bodies touch their bodies. And it reached such a degree of compassion among themselves that no believer would see another believer without shaking his hand and embracing him. Handshaking, the jurists have not disagreed about it.

Abu Dawud related from al-Bara' who said: The Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "When two Muslims meet and shake hands, and praise God and seek His forgiveness, they will both be forgiven."
Page 124

In the narration of al-Tirmidhi: "There are no two Muslims who meet and shake hands except that they are forgiven before they part."

In al-Nawawi's al-Adhkar it is recommended at every meeting. As for what people have become accustomed to after the dawn and afternoon prayers, it has no basis, but there is no harm in it, for the origin of handshaking is a sunnah, and their being observant of it in some circumstances and negligent of it in many does not remove that part from being of the handshaking whose origin the Law has established. Al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salam in his Qawaʿid counted that among the permissible innovations (bidaʿ mubahah), and Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani, may his secret be sanctified, extensively discussed that.

As for embracing, al-Zamakhshari said: Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, disliked it, and likewise kissing. He said: I do not like that a man kiss another man's face, nor his hand, nor any part of his body. Abu Yusuf, may God have mercy on him, permitted embracing. What is related from the Imam is supported by what al-Tirmidhi related: "From Anas who said: I heard a man say to the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him: O Messenger of God, when one of us meets his brother, does he bow to him? He said: No. He said: Does he embrace him and kiss him? He said: No. He said: Does he take his hand and shake it? He said: Yes."

In al-Adhkar: kissing, and likewise embracing, is not objectionable upon arrival from a journey or the like, and it is disliked (makruh karahat tanzih) otherwise, and for a handsome beardless youth it is forbidden in every case.

Al-Tirmidhi related, and graded it good, from ʿAisha who said: "Zayd ibn Khalid ibn Harithah came to Medina while the Messenger of God was in my house, and he knocked on the door, and the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, got up to him dragging his garment, and embraced him and kissed him." Razin added in the hadith of Anas mentioned above, after his saying "and kisses him," he said: "No, except when he comes from his journey."

Abu Dawud related: Abu Dharr was asked: Did he, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, shake hands with you when you met him? He said: I never met him but that he shook my hand, and he once sent for me when I was not at home, so I came and was informed that he had sent for me, so I went to him while he was on his couch, and he embraced me, and it was the best, the best.

This supports the unrestricted statement reported from Abu Yusuf. And it is fitting to emulate them, may God be pleased with them, in being stern toward the enemies of the religion and merciful toward the believers.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abu Dawud related from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, raised to the Prophet: "He who does not show mercy to our young and does not recognise the right of our elders is not of us." Both of them, and Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, and al-Tirmidhi (who graded it good) related from Abu Hurayrah who said: I heard the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, say: "Mercy is not removed except from a wretch."

There is no harm in righteousness and kindness toward an enemy of the religion when it includes a legal benefit, as Ibn Hajar stated in his Fatawa al-Hadithiyyah, so let it be consulted. Yahya ibn Yaʿmar read ﴿ashidda﴾ with a short vowel (qasr), and this is an irregular reading (shadhdhah), because shortening a lengthened (mamdud) form in poetry is like His saying:

"There must be Sanʿa, though the journey be long."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating﴾ is another predicate for "alladhina," or a resumptive sentence, and other possibilities are permitted, as is not hidden. The seeing is visual (basariyyah), and the address is to everyone who is able to. "Rukkaʿan sujjadan" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object. The meaning is: you see them praying. The expression of bowing and prostration for prayer is a figurative metonymy (majaz mursal). The expression with the present tense indicates continuity, and it is customary continuity. From here, al-Bahr said: this is evidence of their frequent praying. ﴿Seeking bounty from God and His pleasure﴾, that is, reward and approval. The clause is either another predicate, or a circumstance from the object of "tarahum," or from the pronoun hidden in "rukkaʿan sujjadan," or a resumptive sentence built on a question arising from the explanation of their constancy in bowing and prostration, as if it were said: What do they want by that? So it was said: they seek bounty etc.

ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read ﴿wa-ridwanan﴾ with a dammah on the ra'. ﴿Simahum﴾, that is, their mark. It was also read as "sim-yaʾuhum," with a yaʾ added after the mim and a lengthening, and this is an eloquent dialect, common in poetry. The poet said:

A youth whom God endowed with beauty when grown, who has a countenance that does not offend the sight.
Page 125

"Sima'" with a lengthening also occurs, and its derivation is from "al-sawmah" with a dammah, meaning the mark put on a sheep, and the yaʾ is substituted from the waw. It is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿in their faces﴾, that is, on their foreheads, or it is taken literally. His, the Glorified, saying: ﴿from the trace of prostration﴾ is a circumstance from the pronoun concealed in the prepositional phrase which is the predicate of "simahum," or an explanation of it, meaning: their mark, which is the trace of prostration. The reason for attributing the trace to prostration is that it arises from the effect which prostration produces. It has become widespread to interpret it as what occurs on the forehead of those who prostrate much, resembling the mark of a branding iron and the callus of a camel's chest. Each of the two eminent men, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn Zayn al-ʿAbidin and ʿAli ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas Abu al-Amlak, may God be pleased with them both, was called "Dhu al-Thafanat" (the one with the calluses), because the abundance of their prostration produced in those places on them what resembled a camel's calluses, which are the parts of its body that touch the ground when it becomes thick. And what is related of his, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, saying: "Do not brand your images (la tu'allibu suwarakum)," that is, do not mark them, from al-ʿalb, with a fatha on the ʿayn and a sukun on the lam, meaning the trace. And Ibn ʿUmar's saying, when he saw a man with a trace of prostration on his nose: "The image of your face is your nose, so do not brand your face nor disfigure your form, for that is only when one presses his forehead and nose against the ground so that the mark appears, and that is pure show and hypocrisy, from which we seek refuge in God, the Exalted." The discussion concerns what occurs on the face of the one who prostrates, who prostrates only sincerely for the face of God, Mighty and Majestic. Some have denied that "sima" means that.

Al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Humayd ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman who said: I was with al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid when a man came with the trace of prostration on his face. He said: This man has spoiled his face. By God, this is not the mark which God, the Exalted, named. I have prayed upon my face for eighty years, and prostration has not left a trace between my eyes. This may be understood as his perceiving that the man did this deliberately, so he denied that what had occurred on him was the mark God named. A parallel to this is what is related from some earlier scholars who said: "We used to pray and nothing was seen between our eyes, and now we see one of us praying and between his eyes is a camel's knee, and we do not know whether the heads have become heavier or the earth has become rougher."

Ibn Jarir and a group related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: This mark is the moisture of ablution and the dust of the earth. Something similar is related from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab. Saʿid ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid that he said: It is not a trace on the face, but humility. In another narration: it is humility and modesty. Mansur said: I asked Mujahid whether this mark is the trace which occurs between a man's eyes. He said: No, though it may be like a camel's knee, and that is harder in heart than stones. It was also said: it is the yellowness of the face from night vigil. This is related from ʿIkrimah and al-Dahhak. al-Sulami related from ʿAbd al-ʿAziz al-Makki: "That is not emaciation and yellowness, but a light which appears on the faces of the worshippers, arising from their inner state appearing on their outer, which is clear to the believers even if it were on a Zanji or an Abyssinian." ʿAta' and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: it is a beauty which overtakes the faces of those who pray. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: the good bearing. And from some of them: "you see on their faces a dignity, because of the nearness of their time of intimate conversation with their Lord." Those who go to these views say that the intended mark on their faces is in this world. Others said: this mark is in the Hereafter. al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, and Ibn Nasr, related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said about the verse: a whiteness which covers their faces on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Nasr, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir related the same from al-Hasan. They also related from ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfi who said: the place of prostration is the most white of their faces.

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and al-Saghir, and Ibn Mardawayh with a good chain, related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb who said: "The Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said regarding His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Their mark in their faces from the trace of prostration﴾: the light on the Day of Resurrection, the light on the Day of Resurrection."

It is not far-fetched that light is a mark on their faces both in this world and the Hereafter.

But because it is more manifest and more complete in the Hereafter, the Prophet (ﷺ) singled it out for mention. "And if a hadith is authentic, then it is my school of thought" (madhhabi).

Ibn Hurmuz read (إثْرِ) with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the thaʾ, which is a dialectal variant of (أثَرٍ, athar). Qatadah read (مِن آثارِ) in the plural.

(ذَلِكَ, dhalika), "that," is a demonstrative referring to what was mentioned of their sublime attributes. The sense of distance it carries, despite the recency of the reference, serves to indicate the exalted status of these attributes and the remoteness of their rank in virtue. It was also said that the distance is in consideration of the subject (al-mubtada'), namely ﴿أشِدّاءُ﴾ ("fierce"). But if this were said, one might suppose that the referent is the last attribute, namely ﴿سِيماهم في وُجُوهِهِمْ مِن أثَرِ السُّجُودِ﴾ ("their mark is on their faces, from the traces of prostration").

(مَثَلُهم, mathaluhum), "their likeness," is the subject, and its predicate is the statement of the Exalted: (في التَّوْراةِ, fi't-Tawrat), "in the Torah." That is, their wondrous description, which in its strangeness functions in the manner of proverbs. The statement of the Exalted (في التَّوْراةِ) is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from (مَثَلُهم), and its governing element is the meaning of the demonstrative. The statement of the Exalted, ﴿ومَثَلُهم في الإنْجِيلِ﴾ ("and their likeness in the Gospel"), is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the first (مَثَلُهم), as if it were said: "That is their likeness in the Torah and the Gospel." The repetition of (مَثَلُهم) is for emphasis on its strangeness and to increase its affirmation. (الأنْجِيلِ, al-Injil) was also read with a fatḥa on the hamza.

The statement of the Exalted, ﴿كَزَرْعٍ أخْرَجَ شَطْأهُ﴾ ("like a seed that sends forth its shoot") and so on, is a new (mustaʾnaf) illustration. That is, they, or their likeness, is like a seed, and so on. Thus the pause is on (الإنْجِيلِ), and this is related from Mujahid. It was also said that the second (مَثَلُهم) is a subject, and the statement of the Exalted, ﴿كَزَرْعٍ﴾ and so on, is its predicate, so the pause is on (التَّوْراةِ). This is related from al-Dahhak, Abu Hatim, and Qatadah. It is also permitted that the demonstrative be a vague indication (ishara mubhama) clarified by the statement of the Exalted, ﴿كَزَرْعٍ﴾ and so on, like the statement of the Exalted: ﴿وقَضَيْنا إلَيْهِ ذَلِكَ الأمْرَ أنَّ دابِرَ هَؤُلاءِ مَقْطُوعٌ مُصْبِحِينَ﴾ ("And We decreed to him that matter, that the root of those people would be cut off by morning").

According to the first and third views, ﴿مَثَلُهم في التَّوْراةِ ومَثَلُهم في الإنْجِيلِ﴾ is one thing, except that on the first view it is ﴿أشِدّاءُ عَلى الكُفّارِ رُحَماءُ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ ("fierce against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves") and so on, while on the third view it is ﴿كَزَرْعٍ أخْرَجَ شَطْأهُ﴾ and so on. According to the second view, ﴿مَثَلُهم في التَّوْراةِ﴾ is one thing, namely ﴿أشِدّاءُ﴾ and so on, while ﴿مَثَلُهم في الإنْجِيلِ﴾ is another thing, namely ﴿كَزَرْعٍ﴾ and so on.

The third view was objected to on the grounds that the basic use of a demonstrative is to refer to something previously mentioned, and a demonstrative refers to something later only when that later thing is a qualifier of the demonstrative, as in ﴿ذَلِكَ الكِتابُ﴾ ("That is the Book"). The reply is that the restriction (ḥaṣr) is not conceded, and the shaṭʾ (shoot) is the offshoots of the crop, as many have said. It is what comes forth from it and branches out on its two sides (shāṭiʾayhi), i.e., on its two flanks. Its plural, as al-Raghib said, is (أشْطاء, ashtaʾ). Qutrub said: it is the thorn of the ear of grain; ten or nine or eight ears come out of one grain. Al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash said: its tip (ṭarafuhu). They cited the verse:

"Let the shoot come forth over the face of the earth,
and from the trees, the branches of fruit."

Abu al-Fath claimed that the shaṭʾ occurs only in wheat and barley. The author of al-Lawami said: the crop sent forth its shoots (shaṭa'a al-zarʿ wa-ashṭa'a) when it put forth its young shoots, and this occurs in wheat, barley, and others. In al-Bahr: the crop (ashṭa'a al-zarʿ) "put forth shoots" when it sprouted, and the tree put forth its branches.

In al-Qamus: the shaṭʾ is the young shoots of palm and crops, or their foliage; its plural is shuṭuʾ. (Shaṭa'a), like (manaʿa), (shaṭʾan wa-shaṭwan) means he brought it forth. Among trees, it is what grows around the base, and its plural is (ashṭaʾ). (Ashṭaʾa) means he brought it forth. End of quotation. In this there is what refutes Abu al-Fath, together with an addition whose benefit is not hidden, so do not overlook it.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn Dhakwan read (شَطَأهُ, shaṭaʾahu) with a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ. Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, and ʿIsa al-Kufi read it likewise, but with a long vowel (al-madd). Zayd ibn ʿAli also read it likewise, but with an alif in place of the hamza. This may be a short form (maqṣūr), or its original form had a hamza, and he transposed the vowel and changed the hamza to an alif, as they said in (المَرْأةِ, al-mar'a) and (الكَمْأةِ, al-kam'a): (المَراةُ, al-mara) and (الكُماةُ, al-kuma). This is a regular (maqīs) lightening according to the Kufans, while according to the Basrans it is anomalous (shadh) and cannot be used as a basis for analogy. Abu Jaʿfar read (شَطَهُ, shaṭahu) by deleting the hamza and placing its vowel on the ṭāʾ. It is transmitted from Shayba, Nafiʿ, and al-Jahdari. Also from al-Jahdari (شَطْوَهُ, shaṭwahu) with a sukun on the ṭāʾ and a wāw after it. Abu al-Fath said: it is a dialect form, or a substitution for the hamza.

﴿فَآزَرَهُ﴾ ("then it strengthened it") means it helped it and made it strong, as said by al-Hasan and others. Al-Raghib said: its root is from tying the waist-wrap (shadd al-izar). One says: "azartuhu," meaning I tied his waist-wrap. One also says: "āzartu al-binaʾ" and "azartuhu," meaning I strengthened its foundations. And (ta'azzara al-nabat) means the plant grew tall and became strong.

Many have mentioned that it is either from (al-muʾazara), in the sense of mutual aid, or from (al-izar), which is assistance. In al-Bahr: (āzara) is of the form (afʿala), as related from al-Akhfash. The saying of Mujahid and others that it is of the form (fāʿala) is an error, because in its present tense only (yu'zir), on the pattern of (yukrim), has been heard, not (yuwazir).

This was objected to: this testimony is a negation and is not heard. Moreover, it is possible that it came from two forms and that one was used in place of the other, and similar cases are numerous. Moreover, al-Sarqusti transmitted it from al-Mazini, but he said: one says (āzara al-shay' ghayrahu), meaning it equaled it and stood opposite it. He cited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"In a bend where the weed has matched its plants,
by the drawing of armies, victors and defeated."

What is in the verse was taken to be of this type. This is also related from al-Suddi, who said: (āzarahu) meant it became like the root in height. The majority view is what was transmitted first. The pronoun in the nominative in (āzarahu) refers to the shoot, and the one in the accusative refers to the crop, meaning: that shoot strengthened the crop. The apparent sense is that the attribution (isnad) in (akhraja) and (āzara) is metaphorical (majāz), and that this attribution is to the cause of an effect (al-isnad ila al-mūjib), which is literal (ḥaqīqa), according to what al-Salkutī held in his glosses on al-Muṭawwal, where he said regarding the saying "your seeing gladdened me": this statement is metaphorical if what is meant is that the gladness occurred at the moment of seeing; but if what is meant is that seeing causes gladness, then it is literal, and its status is not hidden.

Ibn Dhakwan read (فَآزَرَهُ) in its triliteral form. It was also read (فَأزَّرَهُ) with a shadda on the zāy, meaning: then he tightened its waist-wrap and strengthened it.

﴿فاسْتَغْلَظَ﴾ ("so it became thick") means it went from thinness to thickness. This is of the type of (istanwaqa al-jamal), "the camel became like a she-camel." It is possible that what is meant is intensification of thickness, as in (istaʿṣama) and similar forms, but the first is preferred because the context indicates gradual progression.

﴿فاسْتَوى عَلى سُوقِهِ﴾ ("then it stood firm upon its stalks") means it stood straight on its stems and roots. (سُوقِهِ, suqihi) is the plural of (sāq), like (lāba / lūb) and (qāra / qūr).

Ibn Kathir read (سُوقِهِ) with the wāw that is preceded by a ḍamma replaced by a hamza. It was said this is a weak dialect form, and to this belongs his saying:

"The most beloved of the kindlers to me is Musa."

﴿يُعْجِبُ الزُّرّاعَ﴾ ("it pleases the sowers") with its strength, density, thickness, and beautiful appearance. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), meaning "pleasing them." The Exalted specified them for mention because if it pleases the sowers, who know the defects of crops, it is all the more likely to please others.

Here the parable is complete. It is a parable which Allah the Exalted set forth for the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, who were few at the beginning of Islam, then became numerous and firmly established, so that their affair advanced day by day until it pleased the people. This is what some have chosen, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related it from al-Dahhak, and Ibn Jarir and ʿAbd ibn Humayd from Qatadah. They also mentioned from him that he said: "It is written in the Gospel: a people will come forth who will grow like the growth of the crop; from them will come forth a people who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong."

In al-Kashshaf: it is a parable which Allah the Exalted set forth for the beginning of the religion of Islam and its growth in increase until it became strong and firmly established, because the Prophet (ﷺ) stood alone, then Allah the Exalted strengthened him through those with him, just as the first root is strengthened by what surrounds it and what springs from it. The apparent meaning is that the crop is the Prophet (ﷺ) and the shoot is his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Thus it is a parable for him, peace and blessings be upon him, and his Companions, not for the Companions alone as in the first view. Each has its direction. The second was related from al-Waqidi, and a report that Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas indicates it.

The statement of the Exalted, ﴿لِيَغِيظَ بِهِمُ الكُفّارَ﴾ ("that He may enrage the disbelievers by them"), is the cause (ʿilla) of what the speech implies of His bringing them into existence in the manner contained in the parable. The apparent meaning of some scholars' words is that it is the cause of the parable, but this is not so. It was also said that it is the cause of what follows it, the statement of the Exalted, ﴿وعَدَ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ مِنهم مَغْفِرَةً وأجْرًا عَظِيمًا﴾ ("Allah has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward"). For when the disbelievers hear of what Allah the Exalted has prepared for the believers in the Hereafter, along with their honor in this world, they are enraged. This, however, depends on the apparent condition that the disbelievers are certain of the Hereafter and firmly know that the promise is from Him, the Mighty and Majestic, which is far-fetched.

The pronoun in (مِنهم, minhum) refers to those to whom the preceding pronouns refer. The (مِن, min) is explicative (lil-bayan), like its use in the statement of the Exalted: ﴿فاجْتَنِبُوا الرِّجْسَ مِنَ الأوْثانِ﴾ ("So avoid the abomination of idols"). Its coming in this way is not restricted to cases where it governs a noun, as the author of al-Tuhfa al-Ithna ʿAshariyya supposed in his discussion of the statement of the Exalted, ﴿وعَدَ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِنكم وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ لَيَسْتَخْلِفَنَّهم في الأرْضِ﴾ ("Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession in the land"). He said: taking (مِن) as explicative when it governs a pronoun is contrary to Arab usage. The author of the translation (al-Tarjama) denied this against him, but said: if he had claimed this disagreement concerning the pronouns of address and speech, it would not have been far-fetched.

Among its explicative uses governing a pronoun of the third person is the statement of the Exalted: ﴿لَوْ تَزَيَّلُوا لَعَذَّبْنا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنهُمْ﴾ ("If they had separated, We would have punished those among them who disbelieved"), according to those who hold that the pronoun in (تَزَيَّلُوا, tazayyalu) refers to the believers, and not that (مِن) is partitive, as the Shia hold, who claim that most of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, from among the people of the Pledge of Good Pleasure (bayʿat al-Ridwan) and others, apostatized. For their earlier praise, which indicates continuity, such as the statement of the Exalted, ﴿تَراهم رُكَّعًا سُجَّدًا﴾ ("You see them bowing and prostrating"), and their description with what indicates permanence and firmness, such as the statement of the Exalted: ﴿والَّذِينَ مَعَهُ أشِدّاءُ عَلى الكُفّارِ﴾ ("Those with him are fierce against the disbelievers"), refutes the partitive reading and the apostasy they claim, in the view of anyone who has even a little fairness and a trace of religion. Their claim falls even further from consideration because that praise was written by Allah the Exalted in the Torah before He created the heavens and the earth. No intelligent person would accept that He, the Exalted, issued unrestricted praise and wrote it for people most of whom did not remain upon that quality except a few. And if we say that these praised ones are the people of the Pledge of Good Pleasure who pledged allegiance to him, peace be upon him, at al-Hudaybiyya, as the phrase (والَّذِينَ مَعَهُ, "and those who are with him") suggests, especially on the view that the entire surah was revealed upon his, peace be upon him, return from al-Hudaybiyya before they dispersed from him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, then the refutation of that claim becomes clearer and clearer. For the apostasy they claim was for abandoning the pledge to ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, after the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), despite knowing, by their claim, the explicit designation (naṣṣ) of his caliphate, and for pledging allegiance to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. How could that be apostasy when Allah the Mighty and Majestic was pleased with them while they were doing it? The claim that He, glorified be He, was pleased only with their pledge, or with them only insofar as they pledged, and that He did not in general become pleased with them because of it, contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse. The apparent meaning is what was denied. Nor does the occurrence of some sins among some of them afterward undermine this. What undermines it is the occurrence of what is wholly incompatible with pleasure, such as apostasy, and Allah the Exalted is our refuge.

In sum, taking (مِن) as partitive in order to establish for the Shia what they claim is something the Book, the Sunna, and the words of the ʿItra (the Prophet's family) reject. In the al-Tuhfa al-Ithna ʿAshariyya there is, on this matter, what expands the breast and increases the hearts of the believers in light upon light. Glory be to Allah! Where is the making of (مِن) partitive in the claim of apostasy? "And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide." The placement of (مِنهم, minhum) here after (عَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ, "did righteous deeds") and the placement of (مِنكم, minkum) before it in the verse of Light that we mentioned just above are because the doing of righteous deeds is never separated from them, whereas in that verse the purpose is to explain the successors, and righteous deeds are not a condition for the continued validity of their succession, such that they would be removed by wickedness.

Ibn Jarir said: (مِنهم, minhum) means "from the shoot that the crop brought forth," and they are those who enter Islam until the Day of Resurrection. So he returned the pronoun to the meaning of "shoot." Al-Baghawi did likewise, and its remoteness is not hidden.

[Page 129]

This is what is mentioned. In *al-Mawahib* (*al-Mawahib al-Ladunniyya*) it is stated that Imam Malik (rahimahu Allah) derived from this verse the takfir (declaring to be disbelievers) of the Rafidah (the Rafidah, a Shi'i group, are those who reject the Companions) who hate the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. For they enrage them, and whoever is enraged by the Companions is a disbeliever. Many scholars agreed with him. The end of the quotation.

In *al-Bahr* it is mentioned that a man who belittled the Companions was mentioned in the presence of Malik. Malik recited this verse and said: "Whoever among the people has anger in his heart toward the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has been struck by this verse." The takfir of the Rafidah in particular is known from this.

Also, the words of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, point to the same meaning. Al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from her, concerning the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾, that she said: "The Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) were commanded to seek forgiveness for them, but they reviled them."

[Page 130]

It is also reported from some of the early scholars (salaf) that they assigned each clause of the verse to a specific Companion, may Allah be pleased with them all. From Ikrimah, he said:

﴿His shoot﴾ refers to Abu Bakr; ﴿and strengthened it﴾ refers to Umar; ﴿and it became thick﴾ refers to Uthman; ﴿and stood firm upon its stalk﴾ refers to Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all.

Ibn Mardawayh, al-Qadi Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Zuhri in *Fada'il al-Khulafa' al-Arba'a* (*Virtues of the Four Caliphs*), and al-Shirazi in *al-Alqab* (*The Titles*) narrated from Ibn Abbas:

﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him﴾ is Abu Bakr; ﴿are severe against the disbelievers﴾ is Umar; ﴿merciful among themselves﴾ is Uthman; ﴿you see them bowing and prostrating﴾ is Ali, may Allah ennoble his face; ﴿seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾ is Talhah and al-Zubayr; ﴿their mark is on their faces from the effect of prostration﴾ is Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah; ﴿and their likeness in the Gospel is like a seed that sent out its shoot and strengthened it﴾ is Abu Bakr; ﴿and it became thick﴾ is Umar; ﴿and stood firm upon its stalk﴾ is Uthman; ﴿it pleases the sowers, that He may enrage by them the disbelievers﴾ is Ali, may Allah ennoble his face; ﴿Allah has promised those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ is all the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib and Ibn Asakir narrated from him, also may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the words of Allah: ﴿like a seed﴾, that he said: "The root of the seed is Abd al-Muttalib; ﴿sent out its shoot﴾ is Muhammad (ﷺ); ﴿and strengthened it﴾ is Abu Bakr; ﴿and it became thick﴾ is Umar; ﴿and stood firm upon its stalk﴾ is Uthman; ﴿that He may enrage by them the disbelievers﴾ is Ali, may Allah be pleased with him."

All these reports, in my view, are not authentic, and it is not appropriate to apply the verse to them. I hold that each of the Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them, has the fullest share of what it contains. Whenever the seed is taken to mean the Prophet (peace be upon him), Ali's share of ﴿his shoot﴾ is greater than the share of the rest of the Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with him. Perhaps his support and his physical assistance to the Prophet (peace be upon him), by killing many of the disbelieving enemies, was greater than the support of the other Caliphs. Yet despite this, what the verification-minded scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community) held concerning the question of preference (tafdil) is not undermined, as is not hidden from the discerning and noble. So reflect, and Allah, the Exalted, is the Guide to the straight path.

* * *

Among the mode of allusion (ishara) in some verses: ﴿Indeed, We have opened for you a clear victory﴾ points, in their view, to the opening of Mecca, the *ama'* (the cloud or veil of undifferentiated pure being) by the introduction of the immutable entities (al-a'yan al-thabita, the fixed realities of things in divine knowledge) manifest in the light of existence into it, that is, their manifestation to the eye for his sake (peace be upon him). The lam in ﴿for you﴾ indicates cause; the meaning is: We manifested the world for your sake. This is similar to what they narrate of the words of the Glorified: "Had it not been for you, had it not been for you, the spheres would not have been created."

It is also said: it points to the opening of the door of his heart (peace be upon him) to the presence of His lordship, the Mighty and Majestic, through the self-disclosure (tajalli) of the attributes of His beauty and majesty, and the opening of what was closed to all hearts of secrets, the detailing of the laws of Islam, and other openings of his heart (ﷺ).

﴿That Allah may forgive you your sins, past and future﴾: that He may conceal your existence in all times by His existence, Majestic and Exalted. ﴿And complete His favor upon you﴾: by confirming all the good deeds of the world in your record, since you were the cause of its manifestation. ﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾: by calling creation in the manner of both unity and differentiation (al-jam' wal-farq, the Sufi states of union and separation). ﴿And Allah will support you﴾ against the commanding selves (al-nufus al-ammarah, the self that commands evil) among those you call to the truth, ﴿with a mighty support﴾, which few supports resemble. From here it was that he (ﷺ) had the most followers of all the prophets (peace be upon them), and the scholars of his community were like the prophets of the Children of Israel, along with other things that his community attained through his (ﷺ) upbringing of them and his outpouring of lights and secrets upon their souls and spirits. The meaning is: that He may gather these matters for you, so do not be negligent.

﴿It is He who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers﴾: they explained it as something that combines light, strength and spirit, such that the grieving and the distressed find rest and consolation in it, and there arises in them the carrying out of service, the reckoning of the self, gentleness with creation, watchfulness over the Truth, contentment with what is apportioned and withheld, and restraint from gross ecstatic utterance (shath). They said: tranquility descends only into the heart of a prophet or a saint (wali).

﴿That they may increase in faith along with their faith﴾: so there is attained for them the faith of direct vision (al-iman al-iyani) and the faith of demonstrative proof (al-iman al-istidlali al-burhani).

﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾ over all creatures, since you were the first creature. From here he (ﷺ) encompassed knowledge of what no other creature encompassed, because he (peace be upon him) witnessed the creation of all of them. From this station he (peace be upon him) said: "I was a prophet while Adam was between the spirit and the body."

﴿And a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾, since I was the most knowing of creation of the attributes of beauty and majesty. ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are actually pledging allegiance to Allah﴾: this points, in their view, to the perfect annihilation of his (ﷺ) existence and his subsistence through Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is confirmed by the words of the Glorified: ﴿The hand of Allah is over their hands﴾.

﴿Those who lagged behind among the Bedouins will say to you﴾: the ones who held back from setting out to fight the commanding selves. ﴿Our wealth and our families occupied us﴾: the hindrances and attachments. ﴿So ask forgiveness for us﴾: ask Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to conceal those from us so that our journey may be made possible. ﴿They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts﴾: because love of those things is firmly rooted in their hearts and they are not prepared to let anything else enter them:

They were content with wishes and were tried by their portions, and they plunged into the seas of love by claim, but they were not tested.

﴿Say: Who can avail you anything against Allah if He intends you harm or intends you benefit?﴾: that is, those hindrances and attachments will not profit you at all. ﴿Rather, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾, so He will recompense you for them as wisdom requires. ﴿Nay, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families﴾: nay, you supposed that the intellect and the spiritual faculties would not return from the travelers who journey toward the struggle against the self and the pursuit of the spoils of self-disclosures and intimacy, to what they had been upon of perceiving benefits and managing the affairs of livelihood and what this worldly state requires. ﴿And you thought an evil thought﴾ about Allah, the Exalted, and His affairs, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿And you were a people ruined﴾ in reality: perishing in the places of destruction of nature and of bad disposition.

﴿Those who lagged behind will say, when you set out to take spoils, to take them﴾: and these are the spoils of self-disclosures and the gifts of the Truth for the masters of the presences. ﴿Let us follow you﴾: allow us to take your path, that we may attain what you attain. ﴿They want to change the words of Allah﴾ concerning them, by depriving them of the spoils because of their bad disposition. ﴿Say: You will not follow us; thus has Allah said﴾: He decreed and decided ﴿beforehand﴾, when you were in the world of immutable entities. ﴿Then they will say﴾, denying that: ﴿Rather, you envy us﴾, and for this reason you prevent us from following. ﴿Rather, they did not understand except a little﴾: and for this reason they attributed envy, which is among the most detestable qualities, to people of holy souls purified of all base qualities.

﴿Say to the Bedouins who lagged behind: You will be called﴾ and will not be left in vain ﴿to a people of great might﴾, who are the self and its powers, ﴿you will fight them, or they will submit﴾, yielding to the judgment of the Messenger of the intellect, free from the impurities of imagination. ﴿So if you obey﴾ the caller, ﴿Allah will give you a good reward﴾ of the kinds of knowledge and self-disclosures. ﴿But if you turn away as you turned away before, He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾, which is the punishment of deprivation and veiling.

﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾: and he is the one who sees in the abode none other than the dwelling of this world, ﴿for taking part﴾ in abandoning the journey and the required struggle, because beyond that lies [what is greater]. ﴿Nor upon the lame﴾: and he is the one who has lost a complete and sound shaykh, free of defect, in the manner of guiding and bringing to the goal, ﴿for taking part﴾ in abandoning the journey as well. This refers to what they said: that abandoning the journey is better than journeying under the guidance of a deficient guide. ﴿Nor upon the sick﴾ with the sickness of passionate love and infatuation, ﴿for taking part﴾ in that as well, because he is one who is attracted (majdhub), and attraction is better than journeying.

﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾: this refers to those who covenanted to be killed by the sword of striving, under the acacia tree of withdrawal from family and wealth. It is said that much of the verses that follow is similar to this. ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers﴾, the enemies of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in the station of differentiation, ( and merciful among themselves ), due to the strong affinity of some of them to others. Thus they combine the two attributes of majesty and beauty. ﴿Their mark is on their faces from the effect of prostration﴾ to Him, Mighty and Majestic, and the absence of prostration to anything of this world or the next. That mark is the bestowal of divine lights. Amir ibn Abd Qays said: "The face of the believer almost tells of the hidden content of his deeds, and so does the face of the disbeliever."

﴿Allah has promised those who believed and did righteous deeds among them forgiveness﴾: a concealing of their attributes by His attributes, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿and a great reward﴾: which is that He, the Glorified, manifests Himself to them with His greatest self-disclosures, for otherwise everything other than Him, may His majesty be exalted, is not great. And how glorified is He, a merciful God and a generous King.
